For copies of certain papers referring to the School of Musketry at Ottawa.
He said : These are papers in connection with the statement made in this House a few days ago by the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes), The hon. member for North Victoria made the following statement

I have received a communication to the effect that the young men who have come here to learn musketry are being taxed for the maintenance of clubs, for the maintenance of an extra mess, and for extra furnishings generally. I am also informed that privates are called upon to act as servants to officers, and that these young men who are brought from the farms to learn musketry are subjected to prison discipline. They cannot leave the camp grounds unless they get a pass and they must be in at a certain hour in the evening or they are disciplined. I am told that a number of officers and men were informed that they need not bring extra clothing or bedding, but that they had to purchase them here at considerable expense. I do not know whether or not the officer in charge of the musketry school is responsible for this. This officer goes on to say that he thinks the country pays the Cartwright family dearly enough without having the men who come to take the musketry course taxed by this extra expense. I do not think the people of this country want the young gentlemen, privates or officers who come here, to be subject to prison rule. I do not believe that a young man who comes here and chances to be a private, should give up one hour of his time to act as servants to any officer, nor do I think that the country should pay these men to act as officers' servants. I direct the attention of the minister to these grievances which I believe are founded on fact, and which should be stopped at once. I do not ask him to give any answer to-day, as I have not had time to give him notice that I would bring it up.
To which I replied :

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This school of musketry has been in operation for a couple of years, and this is the first time I have heard any complaint. I was not aware that the system in force this year differed from that of previous years. I am sorry that my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) saw fit to make the reference he did to the Cartwright family. I scarcely see what that has to do with it, and I am sure that my hon. friend himself would be the last man to say or to insinuate that any charges that may be imposed on officers attending the school could go into the pocket of as honourable a gentleman as Col. Robert Cartwright is known to be. I am sorry that he made that gratuitous slip. I am very glad, however, that he has called my attention to the fact, and I will make inquiry and be prepared to make a statement on the subject.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, a memorandum addressed by the commandant of the school, Colonel Cartwright, to the Adjutant General. It reads as follows
Rockcliffe, Ont., 14th July, 1904. From the Commandant Canadian School of Musketry to the Adjutant General, Headquarters.
Statement by Col. Sam. Hughes, M.P.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that my attention has been called to a statement in regard to the Canadian School of Musketry made in parliament by Col. Sam. Hughes.
In order that no time may be lost in disabusing the public mind of misconception in regard to the Musketry School, which might be conceived by the public if this statement were left unanswered, I forward herewith for your information :
1.	A marked copy of the musketry regulations for the Canadian militia, showing the camp bedding, &c., allowed to each officer, non-commissioned officer and man.
2.	An extract from the regulations and orders in regard to servants at the Musketry School.
3.	Nominal roll of the non-commissioned officers and men of the Royal Canadian Regiment present at the Canadian School of Musketry, showing the capacity in which each non-commissioned officer or private is employed.
4.	Parade state, showing the number of officers, non-commissioned officers and men at the Canadian School of Musketry.
In regard to the above papers, I might say first that the officers' mess is managed by a committee. Preliminary arrangements, subject to their approval, have to be made with caterers, who have everything in order to proceed with the mess from the first opening of the school. The fees are of the most moderate description and will bear the closest possible inspection.
The staff-sergeants have a mess, other noncommissioned officers have a mess, and the private soldiers have a mess. These messes are managed by a committee, in the same manner as all similar messes are managed in the service. They are spending their own money under the supervision of the adjutant.
Private Soldiers.-There are no privates taking the course at the Canadian School of Musketry. There are, however, privates from the Permanent Corps, sent down to Rockcliffe for fatigue purposes. They are used in various ways, as shown in the attached schedule. It

will be observed that the proportion ot officers' servants to officers is much smaller than that allowed by regulations. It would be a great hardship to prevent these men making extra money as officers' servants, most of the men count on making extra in this way when coming to Rockcliffe.
Bedding.-In regard to bedding, the full allowance of bedding as laid down, has been allowed to officers at this camp. Owing to the fact that at a previous camp officers were allowed sheets and pillow-cases, there may have been some disappointment on this score, but all the officers to whom I have spoken on the subject consider that sheets and pillow-cases are unnecessary for camp life. In any cas it is not a very great hardship for an officer desiring these luxuries to provide them for himself.
Clothing.-In regard to extra clothing, the officers have been given specially to understand that while at musketry work they may wear out their old uniforms. A certain number of fatigue suits have been procured from stores to issue to officers and non-commissioned officers desiring to use them.
When proceeding to Ottawa in uniform officers are required to be properly dressed. As yet, however, the adjutant has not had reason to order any officer or non-commissioned officer to procure extra uniform.
Passes.-Passes are only required for extraordinary circumstances, such as men wanting to stay out all night, or aftr 12 o'clock, or to get off some parade or other duty.
Officers are expected to sleep in camp, as at other camps.
It is, of course, thoroughly understood that officers or non-commissioned officers misbehaving or showing indifference to their studies will be sent home.
The Musketry School affairs, mess accounts, and expenditure are simply arranged and easily investigated, and the more they. are investigated or examined the more the absurdity of the attack on the management of the school will appear.
I do not bear C01. Sam. Hughes the least animosity in regard to the statements he has made, because it is clear that he has been misinformed by some malicious person, who ought to know-, and probably by this time does know, that he has made a series of absurd and misleading statements.
The question as to whether officers attending a course of instruction should be permitted the use of a soldier servant is a matter of general policy, upon which there may be a difference of opinion.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Signed) R. CARTWRIGHT,
Lieutenant-Colonel,
Commandant, Canadian School of Musketry. The Hon. the Minister,
Forwarded. I concur in the above. ''3d.) Aylmer, Colonel, Commanding Canadian Militia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before the motion is carried, I would like to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (.Hon. Mr. Prefon-taine) whether be has any further information on the subject I mentioned yesterday. Is he quite sure that the commission to which he referred, of which the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Copp) is one and some other gentlemen whom he named, is the commission formed for the purpose of dealing with this particular subject and is not a commission formed for the purpose of dealing with some other subject ?

speakeroldname: Hon. RAYMOND PRBFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
In answering the question put yesterday by the hon. gentleman, I referred to the report of Prof. Prince, which is published in the annual report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries for 1903. His report is very voluminous, and goes over the whole question, showing that two years ago this matter was brought under the notice of the department, and a special study made of it by Prof. Prince. It covers about thirty pages of the departmental report of last year. Now as regards the study of this question which has beeii made by Prof. Prince, I will read from his report showing what was done during last year :
In view of the pressing importance of the dog-fish nuisance on the Atlantic coasts generally, the members of two commissions have been authorized to take evidence from the fishermen and report. One of these commissions, consisting of Professor Prince and Mr-Morais, held sittings in Gloucester and Resti-gouche counties in April last, and made recommendations based on the statements laid before them ; but this commission, however-was very limited in its scope.
The second commission, consisting of Colonel Tucker, M.P., as chairman, and Messrs-Copp, Armstrong, Bowers and Venning, with Reverend Father Turbide as a member in respect of the Magdalen islands, held sittings
at various points on the Magdalen Islands and the Bay of Fundy, and as the commission was authorized to inquire into the herring, sardine and lobster fisheries, as well as other important matters, it has been impossible to cover the whole ground as yet, and until the close of the second sittings this summer, it will not be possible for that commission to make final recommendations.
The question is a very large one, which will involve very considerable expenditure of public money to properly cope with it, and it is plain therefore that reliable recommendations can be made only after a very wide survey and a considerable amount of evidence from different parts of the coast has been received.
The erection of reduction works has been suggested, and it is possible that an experiment may be started at once with a view to utilizing the dog-fish for oil, fertilizing ard food purposes, and the department is in communication with important parties with a view to arriving at this end.
The department has already carried on some experiments with dog-fish as lobster bait ; but these have so far not proved very satisfactory, and should be carried on in a more extensive way later in the fall

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: I may add that I have a report of the experiments that have been made, and which are very interesting. Experiments are being carried on on a still larger scale at the present time, and instructions have been given to the men employed on the fishery protection boats to see what can be done to alleviate the nuisance that is complained of. As regards the intention of the government on the subject, it will be seen within the next few days that numerous suggestions have been made. One of them, for instance, was to offer a premium for each dog-fish caught, the premium suggested being lj cents each. While the department were considering this suggestion, we received very valuable information showing that to cope with the difficulty in the way suggested, by offering a premium for each dog-fish, would cost an immense sum of money, and involve an expenditure of over $100,000 a year. The department therefore has come to the conclusion to put a certain sum of money in me supplementary estimates in order to erect reduction works where the dog-fish can be treated for oil and for fertilizing and other purposes. I repeat that the department is fully aware of the importance of this question, and will adopt all practical means to abate this nuisance. In dealing with a question of this kind, certain studies have to be made and certain experiments carried on. This nuisance is not new, it has existed in the waters of various countries, and it has been dealt with in different ways. On the coast of France, for instance, they use the flesh of the dog-fish as food, and it appears that in certain countries the people have no objection to eat that kind of fish. They find it a little coarse, but still it is palatable. But in Canada up to the pre-

speakerposition: stagedirection
stagedirection
speechtext: sent time people have strongly objected to use the flesh as food. Gradually, however, it may be that as a result of the experiments that will be carried on, people may come to find the flesh of the dog-fish as wholesome a food as some others ; and I think it will be found that the taking of this fish can be made a profitable commercial pursuit. Under these circumstances, I think the House and the country will be satisfied, when the supplementary estimates come down, that we have not ignored the importance of this question, and that we are trying in the most expeditious manner to give satisfaction to the fishermen.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The subject is certainly one worthy, not only of the immediate attention but of the immediate action of the government. The reason I thought it necessary to bring this subject to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, was as I explained yesterday, because I found that on the 2nd of May we were promised the report of the commission within two or three days, and we have heard nothing more of the matter from that time till this. I do not believe that the people of the larger provinces of Canada realize the importance of the fishing industry to the Dominion as a whole. In speaking of the fishing industry, I am speaking of course more particularly of the fishing industry of the maritime provinces with which I have been endeavouring to make myself acquainted during the last two or three years. There has been a great deal of encouragement given to the different industries throughout this country in various ways during the last quarter of a century ; but certainly the inshore and deep-sea fishing industries of the maritime provinces have, on the whole, received as little encouragement in proportion to their importance as any of the great industries of Canada. I hope to live to see the day when the provinces of Ontario and Quebec will be fully supplied with the best fish in the world from the fisheries of the maritime provinces ; and until that day comes, and until even that market is extended much further west than the provinces I have mentioned, I for one will not be satisfied. As I mentioned last year, I think that one difficulty under which we labour in the maritime provinces with regard to this matter is that our fishermen still pursue very much the same methods that they pursued fifty, or sixty, or seventy years ago. Not very much advance as I understand-and I am speaking subject to correction by those in the House who understand the subject possibly better than I do-not very much advance has been made in pur methods of catching fish. Possibly there may have been some advance but not much. But I understand from those who are qualified to speak on the subject that not much advance has been made in the methods of curing the fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I am told by those who are engaged in the business that herring prepared in Norway sell at a much larger figure than our herring, and that the herring caught and cured in Scotland sell at a much higher figure than ours. So far as that part of the industry is concerned, the supply of fresh fish to the markets of Quebec and Ontario has made some progress. But that market is still in its infancy, and it cannot be much improved until better means of transportation are provided than exist at present, and I believe those means can be very much improved.
But this is only in passing. The industry as a whole is in very great danger from the invasion of the dog-fish. I have read the report of Prof. Prince to which attention has been called by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I think he is under the apprehension that the pest may prove only temporary. As a matter of fact it has been scourging the fish and the fishermen on our coasts during the past six years from about 1898 and during the last two years it has been particularly destructive. In order to give the House some appreciation of what this destruction is, let me quote from the report of Prof. Prince, at page 52, of the 36th Annual Report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, for the year 1903. His words are as follows :-
The direct harm that a plague of dog-fish can do is well nigh incredible. Thus in 1882 the pack of cured herring in the Shetland Isles was 134-GOO barrels, whereas in 1888, owing to the presence of dog-fish, the total quantity fell to 99,000 barrels, and in 1889, even lower i. e. not more than 47,000 barrels or only about one third of the pack two years before and representing therefore am enormous total loss.
Then, quoting press reports, further on he says this as to our own fisheries along the Atlantic coast :
Every week brings reports from widely different points about the trouble by dog-fish, which are far more formidable pests by sea than the potato-bug is by land. Therefore some people contend that the government should take the matter up and do something to exterminate the invading swarms of dog-fish, or make them scarcer. Now let it he remembered that the fisheries department is not altogether unmindful of the loss suffered each year from this source. The officials, as we remarked before, have been instructed to collect information and tender advice. That was the proper thing for a preliminary step, and the parties applied to should have responded to the best of their ability, but it cannot be learned that many of them did so.
I may say that as far as I am personally concerned, I have not had the difficulty which Prof. Prince mentions in his report, because I have applied to some people familiar with the subject and I have in every instance received full and comprehensive and very practical reports, some of which I propose to submit to the House before I sit down. Prof. Prince's report is quite exhaustive and it is of course so long that I

could not venture to Inflict the whole of it upon the House. He says at page 57 of the report:
The government has been urged to offer a bounty for the capture of a dog-fish. In some parts of the world dog-fish are caught for their oil, but the industry is not very profitable. It is claimed, however, that if a bounty was offered the fishermen would make systematic efforts to destroy this pest, that as the dog-fish were killed off the value of the fisheries would increase and that in a few years the bounty could be withdrawn without injury to the fisherman.
Then he goes on to mention about a dozen suggestions which have been made to the government. Some of these do not commend themselves to my judgment and apparently they do not commend themselves to the judgment of Prof. Prince. After dealing with those suggestions he goes on to say :
If, as seems clear, the commercial products yielded by dog-fish bring such low returns in the market, that it will not pay oil and fertilizer factories to utilize them, and cannot therefore pay the fishermen to fish for them or even to save them when caught accidentally, then a bounty paid by the government seems to be necessary. The livers of dog-fish bring to the fishermen 25c. per pail and at least 50 dog-fish are required to make a pail of livers, and the loss of hooks, bait, and time, have all to be included, hence only the encouragement of a bounty will ensure the energetic and continuous destruction of these fish. Certainly the suggestions numbered 1, 2 and 3 would probably harm the schools of valuable fishes as much as the detested dog-fish, while the employment of a few vessels or government cruisers would not suffice to deal with so general a pest as the dogfish on our shores. Reliance can be placed only on the co-operation of the fishermen all along the coast stimulated by a bounty fairly and effectively distributed on a workable basis. Unless, indeed, the dog-fish in the meantime take the course they have so commonly done in former times and on other coasts, and disappear as suddenly as their hordes originally have appeared. The problem would then solve itself.
I would also like to bring to the attention of the House, because the suggestions which are here made may be of assistance to the lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries in dealing with the subject, a communication which I have received from a gentleman who is very well known in Nova Scotia and who is very largely interested in the fish business. This is Mr. Howard Smith, of the firm of N. & M. Smith, of Halifax. I asked him in the month of January last to give me his views on the extent of the pest and the best way to deal with it, and Mr. Smith was good enough to write me a letter, dated the 28th January, which is as follows :-
Dear Mr. Borden :-As promised, I send you herewith a few ideas and suggestions as to how best to combat this bete noir of our coast fishermen, the voracious dog-fish. I do not speak from experience as a practical fisherman, merely repeating sundry scraps of information picked up from the hardy toilers on our shores, who, 222".
on good grounds, consider this their worst enemy.
I think that Mr. Smith's modesty has led him to probably undervalue the information upon which he speaks, because I happen to know that he has devoted a good deal of time and study to this question and has taken a great deal of interest in it. He goes on as follows :-
Nor are they alone suffering from its ravages. Reports to hand this year from Norway, state that the fishery there was greatly handicapped on account of the enormous schools of dogfish following the codfish, &c., as they swam over their favourite haunts and feeding grounds. Newfoundland fishermen also view with alarm his first appearance last year in small schools. Our American neighbours have awakened to the injury done, particularly their inshore fishery, and the Gloucester newspapers, and fishing gazettes, cry aloud for government action to eliminate, as far as possible, the evil.
I have lately read that ' Mr. Irving Field ' of Harvard University, under the direction of the United States bureau of fisheries, has devoted the summer to the study of the scarcity of lobsters and their destruction by other denizens of the sea. He has brought out the fact that dog-fish is one of the fiercest enemies against which the lobster has to contend, working more destruction than any other of the finny tribe. This species of shark is very voracious, and is declared to be no small factor in depleting the number of lobsters on the coast.
' Mr. Field by the examination of the stomachs of several hundred of the dog-fish, found that next to the rock crab, and the spider crab, the lobster is the chief article on which the dogfish feeds. In several of the stomachs were found lobsters partially digested, which measured over seven inches in length, and the presence of two smaller lobsters in a single stomach was not uncommon. If this be true, an additional reason exists for making wear upon the dog-fish.
' Mr. Field also experimented with dog-fish as food, and declares it to be an article of great merit. Both himself and colleagues partook of it, and pronounced the fish savoury and palatable. It was afterwards served in the marine biological station to hundreds of students and professors engaged in scientific work, without their knowledge of the species, and all pronounced it one of the finest flavoured of fish. It is a favoured fish with those natural epicures, the Japanese, and it is also used as a food by the inhabitants of the Bermudas, by whom it is called 'Nurseflesh.' The name, and difficulty in preparing the fish is the chief objection to its use as an article of diet.'
I have been repeatedly told the fish is an excellent article of food, if care is taken to keep from deteriorating until cooked. Unless put on ice, it tqrns bad in ten or twelve hours, the flesh being particularly rich. Our herring or mackerel exposed in the same manner would keep at least 24 hours. Its possibilities as an article of food to be put up in any quantity, are yet in an experimental stage. Personally, I think it is only a question of prejudice due to the name and the depredatory habits of the marauders.
One thing sure, and that is, they can be used as a fertilizer, after the oil has been extracted from the liver, and the skin can be dried for sand-paper purposes, the latter giving an almost indestructible surface for polishing. Moreover,

the fins, by simply boiling in water, produce the finest glue. One ounce of glue is said to be obtained from seven ounces of fins.
Now here Is the germ of my ideas. Bonus fertilizing factories, say at the rate of $2 to $3 per ton output, whenever a certain proportion of their output is dog-fish residue ; pay the fishermen Jc. per dogfish to enable them to fit out and attack, this, their natural enemy.
How much ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Smith says a quarter of a cent. I <ft) not know whether that is adequate or not.
That is cheap fishing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is a bounty, my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) must understand. Although my hon. friend seems to regard this as a humorous subject as I have observed by his conversation when I was speaking, let me tell him that this is a subject of some moment to the people of the maritime provinces, and that possibly it would be well for him to try and get a little information on the subject rather than to spend his time in jeering while the subject is being discussed.
It is an inspiring subject.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
For the above remuneration, I feel sure, they would make a dead set on it, and you, or any other politician, instrumental in securing such a measure, would be their ideal representative.
These factories could be under the supervision of the fishery wardens or government fishery agent, in each county, the bonus to the fishermen to be paid through the factory owners, who would be solely responsible to their shippers, i.e., to the people supplying them with the dogfish. They would be remunerated by the government paying them 25c. per 200 for the dog-fish horns, i.e., ic. for each dog-fish, two horns being on each fish). I mention ' horns ' because the tails, heads, or other part of them could be imitated from other fish, not so the horns. These could be burnt, or easily destroyed afterwards.
In this way you would be encouraging a new industry, manufacturing fertilizing, glue, &c., fostered under a policy that you advocate, and the fishermen would be profitably employed when the dog-fish virtually stops ail other work. There is no question of the damage done, which, measured in dollars runs up to the hundreds of thousands.
These dog-fish first appeared on our coast about the time the so called Cape Shore mackerel fleet from Gloucester, came down fishing from Yarmouth to Canso in the spring. The fish seemed to follow these vessels swallowing all the entrails, &c., of the mackerel, as thrown overboard. They usually remain here until the run of fat mackerel in the late fall, principally feeding on what are called ' bait fish,' i.e., the younger schools of herring, mackerel, caplin, &c., and, as Mr. Irving Field states doing irreparable harm to the infant lobster. If this is so, you can readily see the damage done is simply enormous.
I direct attention to this part of the com-mnnication and I have no doubt that many Mi. R. L. BORDEN.
of my hon. friends on the other side of the House from the maritime provinces will be able to substantiate what Mr. Smith says :
Take a case like last year, when the fall schools of fat mackprel passed southward to their winter feeding grounds in the vicinity of Florida (or wherever else it may be). The dog-fish unfortunately infested our shore, and were on the inside of the schools of fish with the result that the body of mackerel kept miles off shore, and the expected harvest for our hardy toilers, passed along, virtually untouched. In former years, with no dog-fish, it was not an unusual thing to hear of 10,000 barrels of mackerel being taken in a day between Halifax and Lunenburg.
Hon. gentlemen will note that Mr. Smith is speaking simply of a single day's catch.
What is the value of a barrel of mackerel ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mackerel have very much increased in price during late years ; my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) can give you reliable information as to that.
The value ranges from ten to fifteen dollars.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That would represent from $100,000 to $150,000 for one day's catch along that portion of the shore between Halifax and Lunenburg. As Mr. Smith explains these fish remained off shore last year for the reason that the dog-fish got between the mackerel and the shore, so that the mackerel were driven off and the fishermen could not catch them. Mr. Smith continues :
The same remarks apply as to herring, codfish, &c. Our inshore fisheries are no longer profitable, and this is the only explanation so far forthcoming.	-
Now, why I advocate the establishing and encouraging of fertilizing works is this. If the fishermen are bonused per 100 to catch these fish, after cutting out liver (for the oil) and Saving the token, i.e., tail, horns, or whatever else it may be, they would throw the rest overboard. Now, bitter experience has taught us that this method of polluting the fishing grounds is dangerous in the extreme, witness the( total disappearance for years from Fortune bay, Newfoundland, of herring that every fall came there in countless millions to feed. The careless throwing overboard of herring that fishermen had caught, attempted to freeze, and weather turning mild caused them to deteriorate, so poisoned the favourite haunts of the fish that they left years ago, and have not yet returned in any quantity, and a most profitable industry was thereby ruined. Most stringent laws in Newfoundland, now govern this feature of the question, and as a result, Bay of islands, Newfoundland, where these same herring now go, gives up every fall from its depths, sixty to one hundred thousand barrels of pickled and frozen herring.
I may say that Professor Prince in corroboration of what Mr. Smith has said,

states in his report, that these dog-fish seem gifted with an exceptionally keen sense of smell; that they frequent portions of the coast where fish offal or dead fish are thrown overboard, and that this practice has the effect of attracting dog-fish to the loca'-ity. Mr. Smith continues as follows :
To come nearer home, and to the question at issue with us. Years a.go the Cape Ann fishermen were greatly troubled by dog-fish on their haddock and hake grounds. The dog oil was profitably handled then, and when the fishery was interfered with by these dogfish, they rigged trawls to catch them for 4their liver alone, throwing the body overboard,-result, no fish of any kind will feed or breed on these fishing grounds.
Mr. Smith continues by saying that if some scheme on this line were worked out, he thinks such progress would be made in exterminating the dog-fish as would before long afford a very desirable relief from this pest. I also communicated with another gentleman in the maritime provinces who has very great experience in matters relating to the fishing industry. I asked his opinion on the subject, and although his views differ slightly from those of Mr. Smith, still, as he is a man of very great experience, and as this question is to be considered by the government, and as I know a number of my friends in the maritime provinces take a very keen interest in the subject, I will read a portion of this gentleman's suggestions to the House, in order that the bon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries may have them before him if he sees fit to consider them, and possibly make some use of them. The gentleman to whom I now refer is a man of the firm of A. Wilson & Sons, of the city of Halifax, who are large dealers in fish.
Is that Mr. Robert,?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Messrs. Wilson, of Halifax, well known fish dealers. My hon. friend is no doubt well acquainted with them.
I am well acquainted with them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend will agree with me that they are men of excellent business standing, and men of excellent business judgment in every way.
Certainly ; that is the case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
and the Mediterranean. We are advised that the dog-fish caught off the cost of Norway are cured and marketed in the Mediterranean ports.
I (think Professor Prince reports that these dog-fish have been caught off the coast of Norway for a great many years, and that not oniy have they been utilized for their oil, but also for food purposes in the manner suggested by Mr. Wilson. This letter continues.
We tried last December to get a sample of these dog-fish sent out to us to verify the fact that they were exactly the same kind of dogfish as we get on our shore, hut were too late applying for samples as all had been disposed of. We think there is little doubt but that they are exactly the same, because we know that what few dog-fish are taken by British North Sea fishermen are identical with ours. We noticed by late editions of our newspapers that the ^Department of Fisheries intended looking into this dog-fish question through or by the biological society during the coming season.
This appears to us to be putting the matter off for another year at least for no earthly good that we can see, and which will work considerable harm as it will give the dog-fish another year in which to multiply.
No amount of scientific research will in any way lessen the scourge, and we think their life and habits are sufficiently well known. Now we would like to suggest the following course instead of that proposed by the Department of Fisheries.
That a sum of say ($10,000) ten thousand dollars be set aside for the purpose of having a quantity of dog-fish caught, cured, dried and exported with a view of making a market and commercial value for any and all dog-fish that can or may he caught hereafter.
That the Department of Fisheries select a thoroughly competent practical fish curer to put. this test through. That he be empowered to select as many competent curers (fishermen or others) at as many different points along the affected coast to supply a stated quantity of properly cured dog-fish under a guarantee of say two dollars per quintal for only fish that come up to the standard. Any badly canned fish to be the canner's loss. These fish to be gathered together at Halifax or some other suitable shipping point for distribution to the different markets as a trial. This would enable the government to use up in the vicinity of 5,000 quintal of dog-fish this year; and if the experiment proved a success in the selling markets, as we believe it would, it would not cost the country one cent, because they would get the total cost of fish back in returns, and would probably do away with the necessity of the giving of a bonus for the destruction of the dogfish by demonstrating that they had a commercial value.
There have been numerous other suggestions put forward for the destruction of the dog-fish, but all so far as we have heard, have been in the nature of recommending a government bonus or bounty without a reason-abe recommendation for the utility of the dog-fish when caught, except that of manufacturing glue from the skin, oil from the liver, and fertilizer from the balance.
This scheme would be workable only at points where large 'fleets operate, because it would only be at such points that a sufficient Mr R. L. BORDEN.
quantity of dog-fish could be had to warrant any concern- erecting and operating a plant. This as you are aware would cover very few points on our coast where the fishing villages are so numerous and yet so small. Then, again, the advocates of this plan assert that a bounty of not less, than $4.50 per ton would pay them, which we conclude means that they would want that bounty paid them as long as they operated.
A bounty may yet be necessary, but we think not. if our suggested experiment is tried in a businesslike manner through a thoroughly competent man.
Then he makes some criticism about the way in which such matters have been handled, which I will not read to the House, I have also made an inquiry of and had a conversation with another gentleman who is very well known in the fishing industry of Nova Scotia-Mr. E. C. Whitman of Messrs. A. N. Whitman & Sons, of Ganso. He discussed the matter with me more fully than he has written to me on the subject. His opinion as conveyed to me in a personal interview was decidedly in favour of a bounty, and the erection of reduction stations in order to utilize the fish for fertilizing purposes, after first extracting the oil, and making use of any other products of the fish that might be commercially profitable. I -may, however, read what he has written to me on these and other matters, in response to my request to give me a memorandum of what he thought might reasonably be done by the .government to place the fishing industry of the maritime provinces on a better basis than it occupies to-day. His memorandum of requirements is as follows :
1st. Improved transportation between the east and the west by better refrigerator cars and faster time.
That undoubtedly is absolutely necessary if we are to supply the markets of Quebec and Ontario with fresh fish, as the abundance of these fish in the past would amply justify us in expecting that they could be supplied.
2nd. Have an exhibit of our fish and fishery products at the St. Louis exhibition.
3rd. Have an exhibit at all important fairs in western Canada annually, and during the exhibition have fresh ocean fish properly cooke'd and tastefully served to visitors.
This is of course for the purpose of impressing our friends in Quebec and Ontario, and especially my hon. friend from Essex (Mr. Cowan) with the advantages to be derived from an occasional diet of fish from the maritime provinces.
4th. Establish one or more experimental fishing stations where the most improved methods of catching, curing and marketing fish may be demonstrated. At one of these stations operate for a year a modern steam trawler (as is now being done by the South African government), as well as a steam herring drifter, to demonstrate whether these

methods of catching fish are as superior here as they have proved themselves in other countries.	j
I believe this proposal has not altogether found, favour with some of the fishermen themselves. They have some objection to or prejudice against it. I am not myself in a position to say whether it would be advisable to adopt it or not ; but the methods of catching fish in the maritime provinces might certainly be improved, and it is beyond question that the methods of drying and curing fish might also be improved, and it only needs a little assistance to the fishermen to enable them to adopt these improvements. The fishermen along the coasts of the maritime provinces are as intelligent and adaptable people as are to be found anywhere in the Dominion of Canada or on the continent of America, and if they are given the means of learning improved methods, I have not the slightest doubt that they will at once avail themselves of them. He goes on to say :
At these stations all waste material, such as offal and non-edible fish should be utilized and converted into fertilizer, oil and glue.
5th. Pay a small bounty for the destruction of dog-fish to the fishermen or to reduction works established to make fertilizer and oil front them.
6th. Enlarge the scope of the biological station and make it a permanent structure on the plans of the United States Fish Commissioner's Station at Wood's Hole, Mass. Make it of sufficient importance and interest to attract each year our best scientific men to investigate the fisheries and to discuss them. I
I have thought that the importance of this subject justified me In bringing these suggestions to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. There is no. doubt that this pest has continued for five or six years and that up to the present time no means have been taken by the country as a whole to do away with it beyond the recent investigations which have been made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. We have not the report of these investigations before us ; but the consensus of opinion, so far as I can gather it, seems to be that in order to accomplish the destruction of the dog-fish, or at least an abatement of their numbers, so that they will not interfere materially with the fish which frequent our shores, some aid by way of bounty or otherwise will have to be given to the fishermen to catch them. That seems to be the consensus of opinion on the part of those whom I have consulted or with whom I have conversed on the subject, and who are well qualified to speak with authority on a question of that kind. I admit that it is not a matter into which the government should plunge hastily. I realize fully that proper experiments and investigations must be had before the subject is dealt with ; but I would respectfully submit to the government, and especially to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that nearly three months have elapsed since his answer to which X have referred was given in this House, and the government seem to be making haste, not simply slowly, but altogether too slowly in this regard. The fishing season of this year will very soon be past, and it is important that some means should be taken to abate this scourge during the past season. I therefore trust that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will give his early and earnest attention to this subject, and if possible do something by which the fishing industry of the maritime provinces will be placed once more not only in as good a position as that which it formerly occupied, but even in a better position. If this is not done, and if the prediction of Prof. Prince that the dog-fish will disappear should prove to be unfounded, the results will be disastrous to a very important industry in the maritime provinces and indeed to the country as a whole; because this industry is valuable not only for the wealth it produces, but also for the hardy race of mariners which it sustains. In view of all these considerations, I trust that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will move a little more rapidly in this matter, and that some effective measures may be taken during the present season.

Mr. Speaker I do not rise to discuss this matter, but merely to refer to a misunderstanding that seems to exist with 'regard to the two commissions which have been appointed. The commission of which Prof. Prince is a member is, I believe, in a position to report, 'and has already reported on this question. The commission of which I am a member is not in a position to report. I may say that we had no means of meeting until after the last session of parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would my hon. friend explain the exact object of the commission to which he belongs ?

The scope of that commission embraces the lobster question, the herring industry, and I think also the dog-fish. ,We only assembled after the close of last session and as matters of great importance had to be attended to in the Magdalen Islands, the commission first went there and settled the question as to the spring season of the lobster catch. We then, in December met at St. Andrews and proceeded to Grand Manan. My hon. friend will remember that last winter was probably one of the worst in the history of Nova Scotia and it was very trying for us moving around in St. Andrews Bay. We found that it was impossible for us to hold our meetings with any success. We then held a meeting at

North Head, Grand Manan and also two meetings at Grand Harbour. Finding that .wo could not make any headway we concluded to adjourn and to meet again at tlie call of the chairman under instructions from the Minister of Marine. It is, I believe, the intention of the commission to assemble immediately after the close of the session and I am in hopes that we will be in a position to make a report that will commend itself to hon. gentlemen of this House, and probably in some way solve this question of the extermination of these pests. There seems, however, to be a great difference of opinion as to how the bounty shall be applied. I do not think there is any question as to the need of a bounty, the great question is how shall that bounty be given. That is the question upon which we shall be called upon to report. I feel as the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) feels, that this is a question of great importance to the fishermen and people of the maritime provinces. I do not agree with him that the Minister of Marine is not dealing with this matter ; I think he is dealing with it in a way that will commend itself to the fishermen of the maritime provinces, but it takes a little time. It is an entirely new question and is one that in my opinion should not be dealt with hastily. The question as to whether the bounty shall be paid to the fishermen direct or to fertilizing factories or in some other way is one that should receive consideration and be dealt with not in a hasty manner, but in a way that will commend itself to the people who are most interested.
Would my hon. friend inform the House who are the members of the commission to which he belongs?

The commission of which I am a member consists of Ool. Tucker, chairman ; Mr. Denis, assistant commissioner of Fisheries, Mr. Armstrong, of St. Andrews, Mr. Bowers, of Westport, Pictou county and myself.

I wish to join the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) in pressing this very important matter on the attention of the government. I would have done so earlier in the session but I was aware that the government were dealing with this question and endeavouring to solve it. As was remarked by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) it. is not a question with which we ought to deal hastily; it is one of great difficulty. I expect that the government are overwhelmed with suggestions to deal with the matter in one way1 or another, but while it is easy to suggest, it is very difficult to apply practical remedy. For example, the editor of the ' Coast Guard,' one of the most important fishing newspapers, has stated that a bounty of one and a half cents per dog-fish would probably involve an ex-Mr. COPP.
penditure of $50,000 a day. That was his estimate, provided that one quarter of the fishermen who might engage in dog-fishing would drop their other work and attend to the catching of dog-fish.
What would be the advantage to the country ?

The advantage of course might be the preservation of our fish. The fisheries are of so much importance that it is worth while spending a great deal of money for their preservation. We have in Canada the most valuable fisheries in the world ; we have a coast line on the eastern shore, between the international boundary and Labrabor, of something like 5,600 miles.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The estimate which my hon. friend has given of $50,000 a day as the cost of a bounty of 1* cents per dogfish. seems to be a very large estimate. It would mean nearly three and a half million dog-fish a day.
That estimate is rather under than over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Fishermen might make a specialty of catching dog-fish rather than other fish.

I am told by fishermen that dog-fish are easily caught. A clever fisherman can catch from 500 to 1,000 a day and with a bounty of li cents per dog-fish he could make good wages. Probably 1J cents would be high. At all events that is the estimate of Mr. Nickerson, who is an expert in fishery matters.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Smith suggested only 1 of a cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They do not charge any export duty on the dog-fish ?

I believe not. The Cape  Ann News, ' a few days ago, said in reference to the dog-fish pest on the coast of Maine :
From indications the fishing industry off the Maine coast will be seriously injured, if not practically ruined for a time at least. This i* due to the dog-fish plague which is beginning to assume serious proportions. The dog-fish increase so rapidly and keep other fish so frightened that they threaten to seriously interfere with fishing for the whole season.
In conversation with the Rockland Star man, one of the oldest and best known fishermen in that section made the statement that unless some way was found to exterminate these pests the fishing interests would be practically ruined.	.
' Something has got to be done,' he said, ' and that right away. It is a matter that will not allow oi delay, but the question is what shall be done ? '
Years ago we had the same kind of a plague with blue-fish. They are just as bad as the dogfish when they congregate in large schools and can drive any fish except lobsters. The latur used to fight the blue-fish just the same as they do the dog-fish to-day. Now, however, you hear practically nothing about the destruction wrought by blue-fish because they do not destroy. The reason for this is that they are kept caught up so close that they*do not have, much of a chance to get together and make attacks on the other fish. The blue-fish has been discovered to be a fine food and there is a great demand for it and immense quantities of it are now sold during the season.
We have gotten rid of the blue-fish and now we have the dog-fish, something just as bad. The question is what shall we do to them to get rid of the pest ? It is known that their flesh is not poison and can be eaten, but on account of its stringy composition it is not popular so it is not very probable that the fish will ever become a great food. They have one feautre of value, however, and that is their skin. This makes one of the finest kinds of sandpaper imaginable. It is just like an emery stone and very smooth. It is possible that perhaps this part might be utilized to such an extent that there might be quite a demand for the fish, but this does not seem probable.
T'lien lie goes on to suggest that a bounty is probably the best way of settling the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do we suffer from the blue-fish?

I believe not, at least I am not aware that we do. I suppose that probably the best solution if it can be arrived at is to make this fish marketable, to find, if we can, some commercial use for it. As private capital does not seem willing to undertake the task of doing that, I think some government assistance should be given. I have also been in correspondence with Mr. Whitman, who has been studying this question for a number of years, and he does not seem to be much in favour of a bounty. I
will read an extract from the most recent letter I have had from him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He was in favour of it when he discussed it with me.

I think he is in favour of it, but I think he feels that it might lead to a good deal of difficulty. In the first place, if you give a bounty for catching the fish you must also find some way of utilizing them. As the leader of the opposition has suggested, it would not do to throw them into the sea, it would not do to pollute the water with them. Consequently you must face this question. What are you going to do with them after you catch them ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There must be some inducement to bring them ashore.

Certainly, and I trust the government will be able to provide ample inducement to the fishermen to bring them ashore. Mr. Withman's letter says :
I am sure this is a difficult matter to deal with. May I offer a suggestion ? Let the department establish at some central point a reduction plant to test what commercial use can be made of these pests. If it is found that they can be profitably reduced to oil and fertilizer it will lead others to undertake the business. The government can by such an experiment prove whether a bounty is necessary or whether a high enough price can be paid for the fish to induce fishermen to catch them.
At this experimental plant some dog-fish can be prepared for lobster bait, some more for export to southern countries, where they are used for food, a few can be tinned and any other possible use for the fish tried.
A plant of the most approved process, The Edison Process, to treat 20 tons a day, can he installed for about $20,000 and would want a working capital of about the same amount to run it for a year.
Now that is valuable information. To erect one of these plants at some point on the coast would cost about $20,000, and for an expenditure of about $20,000 more it could be.run for a year. He does not tell us what the profit would be. If we produced 20 tons a day of fertilizer in ope of these factories, the chances are that it would be a profitable industry and that private capital would be induced to go into it and develop it, provided that the government first took it up and showed that it could be made profitable. I think that is one of the most practical suggestions that has been made. Of course there are many other ways proposed of disposing of thesfe fish. It has been said that they could be used for lobster bait, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries very promptly tested that question. A ship was fitted out with lobster traps and sent along the coast to find out whether these dog-fish could be used for lobster bait, and a return has been made to the department which I have seen, and which shows

that the experiment has not been successful, -that the lobsters do not take that bait tas readily as they do other species of bait that have been used. These experiments of course are useful, but you will see, Mr. Speaker, the difficulty of the situation, and how important it is that all these experiments should be tried, and that all the information we can possibly obtain should be got before any step is taken. 1 have every confidence that we can safely leave this important matter in the hands of the government.

I do not often speak in this House, but when I do speak I generally make myself understood, and am not afraid to express my opinions very frankly and freely. I corresponded with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on this subject, and I objected to the personnel of this commission. I do not think that a gentleman learned in the law, busy at his profession, studying the decisions of eminent jurists both in Great Britain and the United States, is at ail the most fit person to be placed on a commission of this kind. Neither do I think that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Tucker), who has had a military training and whose turn of thought may be in that direction, is eminently fitted to serve on that commission. Do not suppose. Mr. Speaker, that I aspire to be placed on the commission myself. I have a sufficient sense of my own ability to lead me to decline the offer if it were made to me. If the Minister of Railways and Canals wished to appoint a commission to deal with a difficult railway question he would appoint eminent engineers for that purpose.
Do I understand the hon. member to say that he wished to serve on that commission ?

I said that I had sense enough of my own inability to fill that position, and that I would not accept it if it were offered to me; and that, I think, would have been the proper course for my hon. friend to pursue. Now I read the report of Professor Prince, it is an exhaustive report, and he has dealt with the matter from a scientific point of view. He speaks from the experience of a practical fisherman ; and my idea of a commission would be one composed of men trained all their lifetime to the business of fishermen, selected from different parts of the province, and not confined to men from the Bay of Fundy, inasmuch as the difficulty extends oyer the whole coast of Nova Scotia to Prince Edward Island. I had letters on this subject the other day from fishermen in my own county who had taken their nets ashore. They are idle now from the scourge of the dog-fish that frequent the coast. The same nuisance exists at the entrance to the Bras d'Or. Now the main question is, what can be done to reduce this

nuisance, for to exterminate them altogether is out of the question. There are three main ideas held on this subject. One is that they may be used for fertilizing purposes. Then there is the oil. A gallon of dog-fish oil is only worth about 15 cents, and if the government would raise the price of that oil to 25 or 30 cents, at most, the fishermen would catch dog-fish for the sake of the oil and confine themselves to that fishing alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: How could the government raise the price from 15 to 30 cents ?
They might as well do that as give a bounty on the dogfish caught. It is only a different way of expending the money.
How does the hon. gentleman propose that the government should raise the price of oil ?

I have been asked that question already. The government propose to spend a certain amount of money for the purpose of reducing the quantity of dog-fish. Might they not just as well take part of that money and give it to the fishermen, who would then spend their whole time catching dog-fish for the sake of the oil ? They won't do so now because the price is too low. Now the idea that dog-fish can be used for lobster bait is absurd. Lobsters are like ourselves, they have a taste of their own, and they select what will suit their taste and reject what does not. Only in the last resort will lobsters take dog-fish for bait, when they can get nothing else. The fish in the sea have their tastes, and prefer certain kinds of bait to others. The animals on land have their tastes also, and so do we in this House. Now there was an idea thrown out by Mr. Smith, I think, in the report that was read by the learned leader of the opposition, about the quantity of mackerel that would be caught from Lunenburg to Halifax. The dog-fish may frighten the mackerel off the shore so that they won't frequent their old haunts. But the quantity of mackerel that the dog-fish would eat would have no more effect on the great body of mackerel than the flour that the members of this House would eat compared with the quantity that is produced in Ontario or the great Northwest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He said that the dogfish got between the shore and the school of mackerel and drove the mackerel off the shore so that the fishermen could not get at them.

I think there are two things that interfere with our success in catching mackerel as we used to do ; first, as has been stated, the dog-fish drive the mackerel into deep water, then in the second place the purse seines used by the

American fishermen in the spring of the year frighten the fish out into deep water, whereas in the old times they used to trim the shore. A question has been asked about the price of mackerel. Mackerel' is divided into three classes. Spring mackerel, belong to class No. 3 because they are poor and thin. Mackerel that are caught in August are No. 2. They are getting fat and white. Mackerel caught in September, October and November are No.l. There are three classifications depending on the fatness of the fish and the size of them and there are three prices. I have sold mackerel at $22.50 a barrel and the year before last from $18 to $20 a barrel could be readily got for No. 1 mackerel in the market at Halifax. But last year the price was lower. Spring mackerel find a market in the southern states and West Indies and fat mackerel all over the United States. I understood from the reports that were made the papers that some of these commissioners had reported already and had recommended that the tail should be cut off the dog-fish as an evidence of their having been caught and destroyed. I know enough of the dog-fish to know that if you cut their tails off and let them go they will be as destructive as ever. I do not think any person possessing a sane mind would adopt that method of destroying the dogfish.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has misunderstood. The suggestion was that the horns should be preserved for the purpose of identification, not that the fish should be thrown away. Both letters that I have read express the very strong opinion that the fish should not be returned to the water. They mention it as a very great evil that they should be returned to the water.

So it is. Dogfish can be used for fertilizing purposes if the proper system is adopted. I would suggest to the government to have a thousand cans of dog-fish canned at some of our lobster canneries in Nova Scotia, that they put them up carefully and send them as an experiment to China, Japan, India, southern Europe and whatever other countries they think might take them for food. If they found a profitable market in these places or in any other places then the fishermen w ould begin to catch dog-fish, can them and sell them as they are now selling the lobster. These are my theories. Advance the price of oil, catch the dog-fish for fertilizing purposes, can a number of them and ship them as an experiment to different markets to see if they will be used for food.
That is being done now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do they treat them by the same process as that applied to Scotch and Norwegian cured and pickled fish ?

Their methods of putting them up are very different. For instance, our fat herring are split up and their bellies are salted inside before the ilsh are salted. Our barrels are poorer and perhaps some of the methods of curing fish are not equal to those employed in the old country. If you get a Norwegian barrel you can knock it about just the same as you could a stone. It will hold its pickle, but if you roll one of our barrels over a rough place it will become leaky, the pickle will be spoiled and immediately the pickle is spoiled the fish are useless for tbe market. What I have to urge is this: Advance the price of oil, encourage the use of dog-fish for fertilizing purposes, have a certain quantity of dog-fish canned and let an experiment be tried in the different markets of the world. No person from the province of Ontario has the least idea of the destruction to our fishermen and the fishing industry by this plague of dog-fish, and I think I may repeat w'hat has been suggested by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, that it wTould be a good thing if the people of Ontario would adapt themselves to the use of more of our fresh and salt fish. If they did so their ideas would be very much enlarged. They would look better and they

I believe that the government is fully alive to the importance of this question, and that the Department of Marine and Fisheries will lose no time in doing whatever is possible and practicable in the Mr. ROSS (Victoria).
matter. I cannot agree with some of the remarks made by the hon. member foi Vic toria (Mr. Wm. Ross), although he is an old and highly respected member of this House. I am not a lawyer, and consequently I am not prejudiced in favour of that profession, which includes so many respectable members of the community, but still I think that on any commission a lawyer, or any man who is accustomed to collect and collate evidence, is a useful addition to such a body. The members of the commission are not giving their own private opinion ; they are simply meeting the fishermen and getting their opinions ; and any man who has had experience in preparing evidence can put that evidence in proper shape and report to the government. I have one word to say to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with regard to this commission. I understand that the members of the commission have given their services free.
Travelling expenses, et cetera, are paid them.

If that commission is to go on taking evidence, I would suggest to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that one of Its members should come from the province of Prince Edward Island. The fisheries of that province are of great importance, and if the province had a representative on the commission he would be able to give very valuable assistance. In conclusion, I repeat that I believe that the department is seized with the very great importance of this question, and that no time will be lost, no time should be lost, in taking measures to exterminate this pest if at all possible.

This subject came up a year ago, and in the interval the Department of Marine and Fisheries has appointed a commission to deal with the dog-fish pest and, amongst other things, to ascertain the best means of utilizing these fish when they are caught. I have had frequent conversations with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on the subject, and he has impressed me with the great interest which he takes in it. He told me he was awaiting the report of the commission in order to arrive at a conclusion, but I would now remind the hon. gentleman that this is a case of extreme urgency. If we delay taking action, awaiting the report of that commission, and if we are to go into an elaborate investigation as to the utilization of the fish themselves when caught, very irreparable damage may be done to our fisheries. The fall mackerel will soon arrive on the coast of Nova Scotia, and the catching of fall mackerel, I need hardly say, is a very valuable industry. These fish are very capricious, and if they encounter dogfish when they arrive on the coast they may strike out from our shores, the result of which would be that this very valuable fishery would be lost to the province of

Nova Scotia. Let me make this suggestion. In old times the Nova Scotia government gave a bounty of 50 cents a hundred for dog-fish ; a large number were caught, and the ravages of these fish were materially reduced in consequence. I would suggest that, pending the report of this commission, the government should establish two stations for the purchase of dog-fish ; one westward of Halifax, somewhere between Sam-bro and Halifax, to obtain the catch on the west coast of Nova Scotia; and another east of Halifax, say in the county of Guys-borough, to obtain the catch of the east coast. Officials of the department could be sent down there to take the dog-fish caught by the fishermen, and a bounty of half a cent apiece should be paid. I mention that amount, because it was the sum offered in former times by the Nova Scotia government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How long ago is it since that bounty was given in Nova Scotia ?
I think it is more than fifty years ago.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Did it produce good results ?

Yes ; it reduced the number of dog-fish on the coast very materially. There is some doubt as to whether a quarter of a cent per dog-fish would pay the fishermen an ordinary wage but fishermen and pilots with whom I have spoken tell me that a bounty of one-half cent each would induce the fishermen to get new gear and go into the business of exterminating dog-fish, partly because of the remuneration itself and partly because of the benefit which their extermination would be to our fisheries. I would like the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to take that into consideration, and while he is awaiting the report of the commission to consider the necessity of granting this bounty.
