House resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me that the dog-fish pest in Nova Scotia amounts to a calamity. The great fishing industry, which in all probability is the second industry in the maritime provinces, is valued at $14,000,000 or $15,000,000 yearly. I- need not add to what has already been said on that score. With regard to the dog-fish pest, the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. William Ross) and the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Mathe-son), tell me that about the year 1850, when they first engaged as young men in the fishing business, dog-fish were unknown. Other fishermen have told me that between 1840 and 1850 the whole maritime coast was beset with these voracious enemies of the fish and about this latter date they practically disappeared. About 1889 they reappeared along the coast of Nova Scotia, at first in small numbers ; but of late years they have increased to a degree that makes it necessary for us now to endeavour to do something to mitigate the pest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. gentleman whether or not since' the period he names there has ever been a recurrence of them ? It might be interesting to know whether they come at regular periods or not, or whether anything can be accurately known in regard to that.

So far as my information goes, they almost entirely disappeared shortly before 1850, and they reappeared about 1888 or 1889. I remember distinctly when they returned to the coast of Cape Breton. Old fishermen whose recollection went back sixty or seventy years told me that they had not seen them before for about forty years. Since 1889 they have been on the coast every year in gradually increasing numbers. Various proposals have been made to the government for dealing with the pest. Among others it has been suggested that so much per tail should be paid for the dog-fish captured. My own idea, based largely on what I have observed as well as on statements which I have read, is that we should very seriously if not entirely deplete the treasury before we entirely exterminated the dog-fish in their season. However, it strikes me that something immediate must be done. The pest is probably temporary. The fishermen have for a number of years shown a great tendency to leave the maritime shores and go to the United States. What can best be done to tide over the present difficulty and keep them on the, coast, ready for the period, perhaps one year off, perhaps five or ten years off, when the dog-fish shall disappear ? I think the measures suggested by Messrs. Whitman, of Canso, and Wilson, of Halifax, as read by the hon. leader of the opposition, are in the main the most promising measures that have been suggested. 1 may say that similar measures were placed before the Minister of Marine and Fisheries some months ago, and I am pleased to know that he proposes to deal with this matter in a comprehensive way. From the prices that fish guanos bring in the markets of the world, I think that if a large amount of money were placed at the disposal of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the establishment of reduction plants, the country would in all probability sustain no serious loss on that account. It is not unlikely that even after these reduction plants for the purpose of making guano from dogfish should no longer be called for, they would still be of use in reducing other fish offal, of which we must certainly have tens of thousands of tons on the shores of the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: For wliat purpose is the oil extracted from the livers of these fish used ?

Machine oil largely, and I am informed that if subjected to the proper process it may be utilized as cod liver oil now is, for medical purposes. However, I do not speak authoritatively on that subject. While we are on this matter, I wish to bring to the attention of the House-the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has already given it his attention-the importance of providing more refrigeration for the fisheries of the maritime provinces. During the last five or six years we have made some progress. I think some twenty-eight or twenty-nine small refrigerators have been established along the coasts, and there is a demand for more. We shall require in all probability forty or fifty more. But no matter how many are put up, these are only intended to meet the requirements of the shore fishermen. They will never meet the requirements of the great fishing fleet that goes to the banks and the gulf, and I must press on the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries the necessity of making ample provision for this great fleet as soon as possible. I am quite sure that the measure will never be entirely satisfactory until we have three large refrigerators, one say in the Bay of Fundy, one about the Strait of Canso, and one in the gulf, say at the Magdalen Islands. With .these we should also require at least two small steamers of the Scotch steam trawler type, fitted up with refrigerators, to convey bait from the points where it can be obtained to the large refrigerators,' and from them to the different points where it cannot be obtained, and also to convey fresh fish caught off the coast to the Atlantic termini of the different railway systems. And here let me point out to the Minister of Railways that in my opinion, and in the opinion of many men connected with the fishing industry, it is essential that refrigerators be established at the Atlantic termini of the railways. We need not occupy our minds about refrigerators at the great markets, for there they are already provided. I wish also to point out to the House that the importance of this matter is seen in the fact that the Newfoundland government only last winter subsidized an American concern by guaranteeing five per cent interest on the bonds of the company to the extent of $500,000, under an arrangement by which the company provides bait for the Newfoundland shore fishermen and deep-sea fishermen, and purchases an enormous quantity of fish from the N wfoundland fishermen and transports it to the American market. I mention this to show that if we are to keep in the race we must take vigorous steps to place a first-class system of refrigeration in the hands of the fishermen of the maritime provinces. The magnitude of the industry will Mr. KENDALL.
amply justify any such expenditure. However, I know that I do not have to press this necessity upon the attention of the present hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries with the slightest degree of apprehension as to the result; because I am sure that every one in this House is thoroughly conversant with the fact that the hon. minister, since he took charge of the Department	of Marine and	Fisheries,	has
never turned down any measure of great importance that has been suggested to him. It is not long since he instituted in the St. Lawrence river a number of Marconi stations and established from the great lakes to the mouth of the St. Lawrence a chain of acetylene gas lights. And it is only a few weeks ago that he made arrangements to have a system of electric bells throughout the River St. Lawrence -a system which has proved very effective along the American coast. I have no doubt that he will also make provision for the extension of a like system to the maritime provinces and make ample provision to deal with the conditions that now threaten our fisheries. Of course there is always a great temptation to adopt proposals more or less popular in certain localities, but that is scarcely the way to deal with a question so important as this. For my part I have every confidence that the hon. minister is taking all necessary measures and dealing with this matter as its importance requires.

The shore and deep-sea fisheries of the maritime provinces is an important factor in the welfare and success of that portion of the Dominion, and representing as I do the largest fishing constituency in the Dominion is a sufficient apology for speaking on this subject at the present time. The great magnitude and increased importance of this industry, if cared for properly, is such that it demands and should receive the best consideration of the government, and as well the recognition and support of the representatives of both political parties in this House. It is a well known fact that the past few years the dog-fish have taken all but complete possession of our north Atlantic waters, and in the summer season the almost exclusive control. They have appeared the past few years in such myriads that other fish are driven from our shores, and are becoming so destructive to fishing property, such as lines, seines and nets, that fishermen fear to put their seines in the water, when the dog-fish infest these waters, lest they would lose them completely. Even when trawling in deep water they are found to eat the fish off the trawls leaving nothing in many instances but the head. The dog-fish is a menace to every description of fish, and what they can't destroy they drive away, hence during the season when the run of dog-fish exists all eatable fish are driven from our shores, the bait fish as well, hence the great scarcity of bait at this season.

The cod-fishing industry is the most valuable adjunct to the wealth of our maritime provinces, and should be protected in the best possible manner not only by a system of propagation, but by a careful consideration as to how all edible fish can be maintained and become a valuable commodity for export. Our forest wealth to a great extent is becoming exhausted or much curtailed. Our mines have their limit, although the limit may be far removed, but our fisheries may be preserved and made marvellously productive, and as lasting as the hills for all time to come. But we must seek a remedy to see this pest dog-fish removed. I know of no industry except farming, and its kindred branches in which this permanency can be claimed. If all other industries diminish, the sea will continue to yield her increase uudiminished, if methods are employed to remove the dog-fish pest and we adopt the system to keep up the supply of edible fish.
I have advocated in this House bureaus of fishing for the advancement of the fisheries, from which valuable information can be gathered, equally as great as the benefits that are at present derived from bureaus of agriculture, and I cannot understand why a measure of this sort is not encouraged and adapted with a view to the improvement and greater development of our fisheries.
We have been suffering now for a number of years from what is known as the dogfish pest. These fislh are not indigenous to our waters, but come from the south and I agree with those who spoke previously that it may well be treated as one of international interest. In my opinion we should consult with the United States government and ascertain what suggestions they have to offer. As I understand, they have also taken the matter up and have suggested that a certain amount be paid t0 their fishermen for the capture of these fish. But that this proposition could be carried out satisfactorily, I have grave doubts. At the same time we can move independently of them to a certain extent. It would be better, however, if we could have their cooperation, especially as they are as much if not more interested in getting rid of this pest than we are. This pest is looked upon by our fishermen as most formidable-one that must be taken in hand and mastered as soon as possible. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, whom I have interviewed on several occasions, seems desirous of doing what he can and willing to receive any suggestion that may be offered him to get rid of the evil. Whatever is done should be done promptly and we should insist on prompt action. Our forests are diminishing steadily owing to the demands of commerce and the anxiety of our lumbermen to realize on their limits as rapidly as possible. Our mines though considerable, will no doubt some day, happily far removed, become exhausted, but our fishing industry is one that will last for all time. But we require to employ every means to foster it and protect it as much as possible. The removal of this pest (the dog-fish) is one of those means. What we require is to ascertain what remedy would be effective. The giving of a bounty has been suggested. I have inlready suggested that a bounty of $5 per ton should be given instead of by actual count. The removal of the tail of the log-fish and then letting it go would not kill the fish in my opinion. As I am informed by the fishermen, the fish would still continue to live, and if they should die in consequence of the removal of their tails, they would pollute the waters and the remedy would be worse than the disease. The reason why I suggested weight instead of number in giving the bounty is because when a fisherman comes in with a large quantity of fish, these fish are very difficult to handle because their fins and tails are like files and injure very quickly all those who handle them. But if the bounty were paid by measure, then the fishermen would get all they are entitled to and quick despatch. With regard to the suggestion thro-wn out by a previous speaker, that we should utilize the dog-fish as a fertilizer and have one fertilizing establishment that would not be practicable. Why ? Because it would not be possible for those who catch the dog-fish to bring them to the factory to be converted into a fertilizer when far removed, but you would require to place factories at the points where the fishing is carried on to the greatest extent. Canso is an important point, but there are other points which would require those factories equally as much as Canso. In giving a bounty to the fishermen we are not only encouraging the fish industry, but we are benefiting that industry by the removal of this pest and in the course of time might be able to get rid of it entirely just as lobsters are less in number than ever before is due to the overcatch, and to the increase in price and the demand.
I therefore feel that the bounty, if given, should be paid by weight, at such a rate as the government could afford to give. I would also suggest that a bounty be given for the oil. The oil is an article of commerce that can be utilized for mechanical purposes and in other ways. I am informed by farmers that as a fertilizer the oil would not be as good as the body of the fish itself. Thus, according to my recommendation, the fishermen would have a bounty for the quantity of dog-fish caught, and also for the oil that would be obtained from the dogfish. I would also suggest the establishment of fertilizing establishments at different points along the coast so that they might receive a bounty as well. By thus providing for the manufacture of fertilizers the farmer as well as the fishermen would receive that benefit to which lie is

entitled from the bounty for the capture of dog-fish. At present we are compelled to send to the United States and purchase fertilizers. Some fertilizers are manufactured in Canada, but many persons haying practical knowledge of the value of the fertilizers say that the fertilizers which they obtain from the United States, irrespective of the duty are better than those manufactured in Canada. Personally I have grave doubt with regard to that assertion ; I think that cannot possibly be correct, but the analysts would be able to ascertain the comparative values of these fertilizers by the tests to which each class could be subjected. The dog-fish could thus be utilized in such a way as to benefit both classes of the community and I am free to state here that the dog-fish Qould be used as a feed as well. I know from past experience that dog-fish, prepared and dried as it can be with very little labour, can be employed as a feed for cattle-not for cows that are being milked, nor for cattle that are being fattened for beef, but for young cattle, young swine, and horses. If the fish can be prepared in that way I would suggest to the Minister of Fisheries that he also give a bounty of so much per ton for all fish so prepared in that way as an a-rticle of feed. We thus have three advantages from capture of these fish, the bounty for the oil, the bounty for the dog-fish as a fertilizer and the bounty for the manufacture of these fish into a good product. If this idea is favourably received by the Minister of Fisheries then I would say let him act upon it promptly so that the fishermen will' be able to obtain immediate benefit. If the matter is left over for consideration they would not receive that immediate benefit. I am in receipt of numberless letters from parties who arc-interested in the fisheries, who urge very strongly that some action be taken by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. These people will await the disposal of this subject with a great deal of interest.
I referred some days ago to the subject of the preservation of fish in cold storage. I would not now have brought this matter before the House but as our friend from Sydney (Mr. Kendall) referred to cold storage for fish and also to cold storage for bait purposes in Newfoundland for sea fishing, I may say that I feel tliat something should be done in this matter. There is no reason why we cannot have a more satisfactory service than is obtained under the process at present used at North Sydney. I referred when speaking previously on this subject to a system that is employed by Mr. Eaton, the patentor who has informed me that not only in theory but in practice his system has been found to give satisfactory results. Throughout the United States immense amounts of money have been employed in the industry of cold storage, and Mr. Eaton is now having one plant put up Mr. KAULBACH.
at Montreal, another he is arranging for at Toronto and another is about to be set up here in Ottawa. In order that the House may have a clear idea of the advantages of this system, I shall read to the House the prospectus of the Eaton Company :
Are these plants being put up in Ottawa and Montreal by the government or by private individuals ?
Private individuals, capital subscribed. The prospectus is as follows :

speechtext:
Ice of absolutely pure quality and free from bacteria, can be made in large quantities by the Eaton process for 10 cents per ton laid down in the icehouse.
Present cost of production.
Ice of much inferior quality, such as is obtained from the St. Lawrence or Back river, costs 75 cents per ton laid down, and is sold by the trade to large customers at $2 to $3 per ton, delivered at their place of business.
Comparative qualities.
While all river or lake ice, even the very finest, contains great numbers of germs and impurities dangerous to the health, Eaton ice is absolutely free from both, being made from water which has undergone careful scientific Alteration. Nor does it contain air-bubbles, which in the ordinary article cause a loss of 40 per cent by melting, Eaton ice is hard as flint, so hard that it has a metallic rirg, and it can neither rot nor become honeycombed. The absence of imbedded air prevents it from melting and from creating any moisture, it can only evaporate from the outside. Thus while dealers now are compelled to lay in a stock of 8,000 tons of ordinary ice for every 5,000 which they deliver during the season in order to effect a clear loss of 3,000 tons by melting, no loss of any consequence would occur with the Eaton ice, the loss by evaporation being merely nominal.
Absolute certainty of supply.
Ice famines are of no infrequent occurrence, owing to mild winters which do not permit the formation of cakes sufficiently thick to survive the storage period. The thinner the cakes of ice which are collected from the river, the greater will be the subsequent loss from melting in the icehouse during the summer.
The Eaton process obviates this danger in its entirety, while cold weather enables the process to be worked to the best advantage, there is no necessity for greater cold than that of the ordinary freezing weather which prevails in Canada for several months in the year. At a temperature 25, or 26 F or 30 or 40 C., one half inch of ice can be made per hour or 12 inches in 24 hours. With lower temperatures, it is made correspondingly faster. The horizontal dimensions of the ice cake are of course, limited only by the space available for the ice-bed and by the amount of the water supply. This would seem to prove that Canada is the country par excellence for working the Eaton process.

Actual cost of making ice in 8,000 ton house is therefor 71 cents. To this must be added the interest charges on outlay for ground and plant. Larger plants will work cheaper still, because a considerable saving can be made in the cost of building and wages.
Plant and machinery.-The Eaton process works entirely without chemicals or machinery. Nature alone does the work of freezing. An expensive plant, therefore, is unnecessary; only, houses to store the ice, with a water power attached to each for the treatment of the water, all built of 'the plainest materials. A 20.000 tons plant can be put up in this city lor about $10,000, and larger plants propor-tionably cheaper
Size of Canadian market.-According to carefully collected statistics, there are consumed annually in the city of Montreal, at least 500,000 tons of ice, and in Toronto double that quantity, while the joint consumption of the lesser cities may be put down at another '$500,000 tons, or at least 2,000,000 tons per annum, in Ontario, Quebec and the lower provinces. This is believed to be a very conservative estimate. Besides this local consumption, there is an unlimited Held for export . for if the city of Portland, Maine, can export 5,000,000 tons of ordinary >ice per season. ice which has to be brought 160 miles by rail, leaving 50 per cent of its substance in transit, there is manifestly no reason why St. Jrhi. and Halifax could not build up a large business by shipping Eaton ice made at the wharfs and losing only a paltry percentage by evaporation. Ordinary good ice sold during the hot season, commands as much as $20 per ton at New Orleans, and $12 to $15 per ton at St. Louis ; France and England, too, are ready to pay high prices for good ice.
Canadian company to work the Eaton process [DOT]-Mr. Eaton is the sole owner of the patents covering his process of making ice and handling water in Canada He has conveyed to the Union Ice Co., Canada, the sole right to use his process in the province of Ontar'o, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island for the full term of the life of the patents. He has undertaken also to give to this company the free uses of any further improvements which he may make in his process, for the above territory.
The capital of the Union Ice Company is $500,000 in 100,000 shares of the par value of $5 each, fully paid and non-assessable. If a suitable property can be acquired, and a
20,000 ton plant erected, which can he done easily In three or four weeks, so as to be ready for the first cold weather in January, the house ought to be filled with ice before January 1st. 'When this has been done, the local ice trade can be given an opportunity to examine into the quality of the ice, the working of the process, the cost of production, and their own chances of competing with a system which works far cheaper and more certainly than the river. There being no desire to interfere with their trade, they can be offered all the ice they want at a figure considerably below what they are. paying now ; the stock necessary to fill their contracts can he carried for them in the company's houses until delivery time, and thus they will be saved the large outlay in cash for sawing, carting and packing, which they now must lace every winter. If they decide to act thus as distributors of ice only, they will be able to get along without their icehouses and may realize upon their real estate' and buildings. These inducements are thought to be so palpably plain that the trade will become at once the company's customers and all enmity and ill-feeling will be avoided.
I must apologize. Mr. Speaker, for occupying the time of the House in reading this lengthy description of the system of ice production. I may say also that Mr. Eaton has described to me the virtue of the ice that is thus made. He says that the water goes through an electric process which deprives it of all the germs that water would naturally possess. The ice thus formed is therefore clear of all impurities of every description, and retains its congealed quality much longer that if it had not undergone this electric process. He further says in his prospectus that it removes all air globules from t'he ice. which in ordinary ice have a tendency to destroy the fish or meat when it is brought in contact with them. He further says, as I have remarked on a previous occasion in speaking on this subject. that the ice made by this process retains all the phosphoric properties contained in the fish or meat ; whereas by the ordinary process of packing these articles in ice, those properties disappear much sooner. He also states that fish when deprived of its phosphoric properties is worthless, even as bait, and the fish will not take it. He goes on further to say that when ordinary bait is removed from the icehouse and taken on board a fishing craft, the bait will last but a very short time, whereas by his process it will last considerable longer. He also told me that he would think nothing of wrapping a pound of ice in a piece of thick paper, putting it into his satchel and travelling to Boston and back, and the ice would he in almost as perfect a condition as when he started. If that is the case it certainly offers many advantages over any other method of manufacturing ice that I have yet heard of. I have occupied a considerable time in givin expression to my views in regard to the question of dog-fish and

speechtext: the remedy to be applied for the purpose of securing the removal of this pest with which tlie fishing industry of the maritime provinces has to contend. I sincerely hope the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will seriously take the matter into his consideration and act in a prompt manner in order that the fishermen of the maritime provinces may have the encouragement which they anticipate they will receive from the bounty which I suggest. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the interest in this subject may be limited to a number of members in this House, I think its importance to the maritime provinces fully justifies the time and attention that have been given to it to-day. As the representative of a fishing constituency and as a minister from the maritime provinces, I naturally have the warmest interest in the subject.^ I have had much correspondence concerning it with people in the fishing business, including some of the gentlemen whose names have been mentioned in the discussion to-day and whose large experience entitles their opinions to the utmost consideration. I have repeatedly been in communication with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) on the subject, who at all times has manifested the warmest interest in the matter and the strongest desire to bring about some satisfactory solution. As he has indicated in the answers which he has given to questions which have been asked during the session, difficulties have been met with owing to the wide differences of opinion as to what is the best mode of dealing with the evil. That the evil exists, and that it is a great one, is fully realized, but the proper method of dealing wtth the matter is a question which necessarily requires time for consideration. 1 can only say that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has repeatedly' assured me that it is his desire to co-operate with the maritime representatives in the matter, and when I came recently to prepare the supplementary estimates for the current year, which are not yet before the House, the hon. minister asked me to include a considerable sum to enable him to carry on some experiments along the line of what has been the general expression of opinion this afternoon ; that is, the establishment of reduction works for the treatment of dog-fish, both as to the preparation of the dog-fish as *a food product and as to the production of Mr. KAULBACH.
oil and fertilizers. I can assure my bon. friends opposite, who have spoken on the subject, that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is entirely in sympathy with all that has been said, and has given the most substantial evidence of that fact by asking me to give him the necessary appropriation to carry out these proposed experiments.

Mr. Speaker, L would like to ask the hon. Minister of Fin ance if any attempt has been made to establish a cold storage service once a week between the maritime provinces and the province of Ontario. I allude now to the transportation of such fish as kippered herring and finnan haddies. I do not allude to those kinds that are in tin cans, but I refer to the kinds that are packed in boxes. We begin to receive them from the maritime provinces, St. John particularly, in November. They begin then to send them to us by express. The express companies have given us a very low rate on fish, but the difficulty is that we cannot get them at every season of the year. If the Lenten season is very late in the spring, we want a supply of fish, and to get this supply we must have a cold storage service from the maritime provinces to Ontario. If a car came up once a week, leaving St. John or some other maritime port every Wednesday or Thursday so that we could have the fish here by Friday, and we knew that a car was coming every week, it would be a great advantage to us. We are anxious to receive this fish in Ontario. We cannot get them unless we get them from the maritime provinces, and why can we not have fish the same as the people in the maritime provinces have ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Something has been done along the lines suggested by my hon. friend, but there is ample room for expansion , as he has suggested. The Intercolonial Railway, and I think the Canadian Pacific Railway, are providing some facilities for bringing fish in cold storage, but I believe that tlie opportunities for an expansion of this business in the upper provinces are very great indeed, and I am delighted to hear my hon. friend say that the people of Ontario are looking forward to obtaining supplies in that way. Something has been done, but there is ample room for improvement on the part of both of the railways.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am told that an express car is run from Vancouver to Boston, attached to the Imperial Limited, which carries an enormous mass of halibut every day in the week, and surely if this can be carried all the way from British Columbia to Boston and sold at remunerative prices, the fish of the maritime provinces could be taken to Ontario, Quebec and even farther west.

Mr. Speaker, I think the discussion which has taken place to-day

must be productive of great good, because there seems to be but one opinion on both sides of the House, and that is that everything possible should be done for the benefit of this great industry- The fishing industry of the Dominion of Canada is worth about 823,000,000 annually. The fishing industry of the province of Nova Scotia is worth some $8,000,000 annually, and an industry of those proportions in a province of the size of Nova Scotia is one of very great importance indeed. I am sure that we are all anxious that it shall be fostered in every conceivable way, and I am glad to say that in all the communications I have had with the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. PrSfontaine) and his officials, they have always manifested the greatest interest in this industry and the desire and determination to do all they can to benefit it. In regard to the fishing industry as a whole, one of the great questions in connection with it is the transportation question. There is no doubt about that. If you have fish ir the maritime provinces and you have consumers in Ontario, you must have means of transportation in order to get the fish from one place to the other. Unfortunately in Nova Scotia large sections of the fishing country have been deprived of transportation facilities, particularly from Halifax to Barrington and Yarmouth, and from Halifax east to the Strait of Canso. But it will only be a short time until we have a railway in operation along the southwest coast of Nova Scotia, and I trust that in the near future we will have a railway to the east from Halifax to the Strait of Canso. Then, with refrigerator cars, it will be possible to send large quantities of fresh fish to the markets of the west.
In regard to the methods that are being pursued at the present time, although the methods have been improved very considerably, I think it will be necessary in the near future for the fishermen of the maritime provinces to make very radical changes in the methods they have been pursuing because of the change in the market. They have to turn to the home markets more than in the past, because the West India markets, for reasons which I need not now stop to mention, are being lessened. 1 Already this work has been begun, and firms are being established to prepare fish in the most attractive forms, and they are shipping as far west as Winnipeg and Regina. I agree that while the fisheries in Nova Scotia are worth $8,000,000 annually there is no reason why, with certain improvements, these fisheries could not be made to be worth at least $15,000,000 per annum in a very short time. That is a very great consideration. To illustrate that, I may say I know of a locality in my own county which is bordering on the Bay of Fundy. A few years ago I suppose the whole output from this one settlement was not more than- $500 or $000 a year. But a pier has been erected at this place, which enables the fishermen to carry 2231
on their industry during the winter, which is the time for the haddock fishery, and as a result the output from that place is something like $20,000 a year.
The government is every year providing facilities to enable the fishermen to more profitably prosecute their calling. The result in the place I have mentioned is that we have received back in return more than $20,000 per year, and wherever that can be done the industry will be stimulated. I am glad that parliament is so alive to the great disadvantages our fishermen are labouring under because of the presence of these dog-fish. For some two or three years I have had my attention called to this matter very closely ; I have had communications with fishermen and with fish dealers, and with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the officers of his department. Everybody recognizes the evil, but the great question has been how it can be remedied. The government has been ready to do everything it can do, but the question remains what shall be done ? There has been a difference of opinion, and that is natural because people cannot very well decide how it is possible to provide a remedy. Many intelligent people tell me it is idle to think of exterminating the dog-fish ; others think they can be exterminated. There is a great deal of capital invested in the shore fisheries and a great many men are dependent on these fisheries for their livelihood. During the season this dog-fish scourge is on, these men are absolutely unable to earn a dollar. They go out in their boats and attempt to fish, but the lines are seized by the dog-fish and cut and the hook carried away, so that it is impossible for the fishermen to pursue their calling. If some means were adopted by which the fishermen during this season could catch dog-fish and make a small wage, even if it were only a dollar a day, it would save them from actual want which often results now. I have had extensive correspondence about this matter with people who are in a position to know, and I think the consensus of opinion among the best informed people is, that the government should do something in the way of aiding the erection of reduction works in eeftain localities along the coast. It would not be necessary for these reduction works to be so very close together, because the fish could be gathered up and delivered to them. The reason I think it would be necessary for the government to assist in this enterprise, is because of the uncertainty of a continuance of this dog-fish evil. They have been here before and have suddenly disappeared and that may happen again at any time let us hope it will happen soon-but that uncertainty is sufficient to deter private capital from engaging in the establishment of reduction works. I therefore think that if the government would assist a private company in the erection of their plant,

requiring them in return to take all the 'dog-fish offered at a stipulated price, the most good could be accomplished. Then, whether the dog-fish were present or not, the fishermen would be enabled to earn a livelihood. I am satisfied that these reduction works could be made substantially self sustaining, but even suppose there was a considerable loss, the government is assisting other industries and it is but right that our great fishing industry should be assisted also. It is a matter for congratulation that there is on this question such a unanimity of opinion in this House ; and that we are all actuated by the one desire to support the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in an earnest endeavour to exterminate this plague and to give courage to our fishermen who'have been so tortured by it in the past.

I would not venture to occupy the time of the House were it not that my constituents are deeply interested in this question. I can heartily endorse the remarks of the leader of the opposition, and also the remarks made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House in reference to the importance of our fisheries and the necessity of their preservation. I have the honour to represent a fishing constituency which represents one-third of the fishing industry of the province of New Brunswick; the total value of the fisheries of that province being about $4,000,000 of which $1,500,000 comes from the county of Gloucester. The fishermen of my county have suffered as well as the fishermen of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island from this dog-fish pest which has been engaging the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and his department for the last year or two. In the waters frequented by the fishermen of my county on the Prince Edward Island banks as well as along the aorth shore of New Brunswick, these dog-fish have been in existence for over forty years, but until recently in such small numbers that the attention of the fishermen was not particularly attracted to them. Last year, after the first of August the fishing industry carried on in Gloucester county by over 220 fishing vessels virtually ceased, and evidence was given before the commission to show that the resultant loss amounted to over $50,000. The fishermen of my county have urged upon me the necessity of asking that the government shall come to their assistance. Last winter the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was kind enough to appoint what I might call a local commission, consisting of Professor Prince, and Mr. Pierre Morais, of Caraquet, to take the evidence of the fishermen in that district. When we realize that the products of the fisheries amount to $15,000,000 in the maritime provinces, and to $23,000,000 in the whole Dominion, it is easy to see what a great necessity there is for preserving this in-Mr. WADE.
dustry. I believe that with an earnest effort to develop our Canadian fishing industry it could be made to double in value within the course of a few years, so that New Brunswick would produce $8,000,000 or $10,000,000 ; Nova Scotia, $25,000,000 or $30,000,000, and the whole Dominion of Canada, $50,000,000, instead of $23,000,000 as at present. I am glad to say that the government is showing an interest in this matter and that their desire is to encourage the fishermen of the maritime provinces. For a number of years past we have had larger and more numerous appropriations for the construction of breakwaters and lighthouses, all calculated to facilitate the fishermen in the pursuit of their calling so that they may now get in and out of the harbour at night time as well ns in the day. at low tide as at high tide. Instead of having to leave the banks on Friday night or early Saturday morning as was the case a few years ago. in order to get home for Sunday, the fishing fleet can now engage in fishing for a part of the day on Saturday, knowing that in view of the advantages that have been conferred upon them by the government, they can come into the harbour at night, and thus they have more time to prosecute their operations.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has certainly shown great interest in dealing with this calamity by appointing commissioners on the subject. While these commissioners have not yet reported, a number of suggestions have been made of more or less practicability. Some of them may be practicable along certain portions of the coasts of the maritime provinces while not practicable along other portions. Some suggestions have been made in this House and outside of this House, which may be practicable along the coast of Cape Breton, but not practicable for the fishing fleet of the county of Gloucester, which is isolated from the other fishing fleets of the maritime provinces. Every means which can be devised to diminish the dog-fish calamity Should be taken as far as practicable. Among the suggestions which have been made is the establishment of fertilizers. I believe in the establishment of these fertilizers along our coasts, and I am surprised that the people of Canada have not sooner realized their necessity. At the same time, if we wait until these fertilizers are ready to do the good work they are likely to do, perhaps our fishermen will have lost patience and will have abandoned the fishing industry entirely. The men engaged in the fishing industry are laborious and active, and, as the hon. leader of the opposition said this morning, their valour and intelligence can be appreciated as well as the valour and intelligence of any other class of the Canadian people. They are willing to grapple with any difficulty and
roi3

aelp themselves out of the difficulty. It has iJso been suggested that a bounty should be said to the fishermen, varying in amount. *Such a bounty seems at first sight to be extravagant, and likely to bring Canada into i very large expenditure. It cannot be so, is our fishermen would only devote to dog-ish time that could not be otherwise utilized ,vhen at sea, on the fishing banks. Our deep-sea fishermen have no ambition to become ishers of dog-fish for the rest of their lives. 1'hey are anxious that the dog-fish pest shall 33 exterminated without their assistance, if oossible. It has been suggested also that the government cruisers employed in projecting the coasts of the maritime provinces should be equipped in order that they may eapture dog-fish in large quantities. They might be equipped with large -seines of strong cord, similar to those which the Americans used in depleting our waters of mackerel and other fish at the time of the Washington treaty. If those men were able with their destructive engines, to destroy such fish as mackerel, we ought to be able ;o -find means for destroying the_ dog-fish, which is threatening to destroy our shore fisheries. I would suggest co-operation between the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the fishermen of the county of Kloucester and of the maritime -provinces it large. I am sure the Minister of Marne and Fisheries has at his command men of ability, energy and tact, who would be willing to give their services and their best ibility to the large interests of the country, nen like Commander Spain and Commander Wakeham, placed at the head of such a fleet, would, I am sure, in the course of a few weeks show, to the advantage of Canada and the advantage of the fishing interests of the maritime provinces, that their efforts would be worth the small expenditure they would cost. I understood that the sum of .$25,000 lias been placed at the command of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for this emergency. The hon. minister has already assured us that he is ready to combat any imergency, and I believe he is as willing and ready to combat this emergency of the dog-fish calamity, in the interest of the fisheries of the maritime provinces, as he has been to equip the gulf and river St. Lawrence -for navigation. For the destruction of the dog-fish pest prompt and vigorous action is required. Our fishermen cannot afford to wait for three or four years, for in tha-t time, in their ambition, they will certainly leave the country and look for better employment ; and once they leave they will not come back to that industry. We are exerting ourselves to promote the interests of our fishermen. The people of Montreal, Toronto and the west are asking for the fish of the maritime provinces. Let us show our fishermen that they, will be encouraged as well as the men of any other industry. 1 believe that a large amount should be placed at the disposal of the
Minister of Marine and Fisheries. If he does not find the necessity of expending it, he need not expend it ; but it should be there for the occasion. I believe that practical suggestions will be found only as the department engages in the work and looks l'or practical suggestions-it is only when you are at work that the best suggestions come to you ; and I believe the suggestions will receive consideration, not only from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but from his hon. colleagues in the Council and from every member of this House.

Mr. Speaker, just one word with regard to this very important subject. No member of this House need apologize for calling attention to the importance of an industry which amounts to something like $22,000,000 or $23,000,000 annually to -the Dominion of Canada, Representing, as I do, a very important constituency, containing as it does a seacoast ot about 150 miles, containing also a very important salmon-fishing river, I do not feel that I should apologize for a moment for making a few observations in reference to this matter. With regard to this last commission that has been appointed, I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Victoria (Hon. Wm. Ross) in objecting to the personnel of that commission. I think the personnel of the commission is all right, but it is important to take into account the local conditions in various parts of the country. When our fishing industry is scattered along 5,000 miles of coast, it is obvious that a commission picked from one locality would not be calculated to understand local conditions so readily as a commission picked from the various localities along the coast.
I find, on looking over the personnel of the commission then, that it is composed of gentlemen representing the Bay of Fundy constituencies and the Department of Marine and Fisheries. And if there is to be any change made in its personnel, my oniy suggestion would be that it should be * composed of gentlemen taken from the various parts of the coast, leaving the selection to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries and his colleagues. I must say in passing that I can only add my mede of praise to the conduct of the hon. minister in connection with the duties pertaining to his office. I would call attention particularly to one feature in his administration and that is that he is always ready Ho get rid of ' red tape ' and deal with a measure upon its merits. That certainly has been my experience, and that certainly is a feature of the hon. gentleman's administration well worthy of commendation. As this dogfish pest has assumed such serious proportions as to become a menace to a most valuable industry, there is no need for me to say anything regarding the urgency of our doing something to extirpate it. What re-

quires to be done is for each gentleman from the maritime provinces to offer suggestions as to the means he considers best to get rid of the pest. It has been suggested that a reduction factory should be established for the purpose of enabling this fish to be utilized as a fertilizer, and according to the estimate of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that would cost something like $20,000 for the plant and $20,000 to run it. I am told that this is a very moderate estimate, and I observe in this connection that while the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche) agrees to this proposition, he couples his endorsation of it with the suggestion that the experiment should be tried on the Halifax coast. He leaves out of consideration the fact that we have a coast of something like 5,000 miles to deal with and that the dog-fish are not disposed to remain on the coast of Halifax any longer than anywhere else along our shores. It may then be urged that if the visits of these fish are of so transitory a character, why make so much ado about them. Well, one week of the dog-fish around our coast" means perhaps two months destruction of our fisheries. Not only do these destroy the fishing lines, but also all the fishing nets and what is more it is well known by fishermen that the presence of this pest on the coast for one week will scare away all species of other fish for weeks at a time. Therefore do I say that the presence of this pest on our coast for one week might lead to the destruction of our fish for two months possibly.
BORDEN. But they do stay much longer.

Yes, unfortunately they do, but I am merely supposing a case. An<T I say that the transitory character of their visits would certainly tell very much against the establishment of a permanent institution such as a reduction plant. For the past thirty years I have lived among the fishermen and frequently have talked this subject over with them and the conclusion I have come to is that the best way to meet the evil would be to grant such inducements to destroy the fish-would be to give a bonus for every gallon of dog-fish oil sent to market or reduced or so much per head for every fish caught. That would be much more effective than a reduction plant, inasmuch as tt would cover our whole coast. It might be said that an army of officials would be required to check the counting of these fish, which would certainly be an objection, but at the same time I am sure that the money -we would spend in a month or so in this way would be much more than compensated for by the additional value given to our fisheries. I would therefore urge upon the minister and his colleagues the advisability of experimenting along this line and to pay a bounty Mr. Mclennan.
either of so much per fish caught or so much a gallon for every gallon of oil. TWo most important classes would in this way be benefited, because after the oil would be taken from the fish the residue would make a capital compost to be used on farm lands, and I venture to say that this compost would find a ready market, so that the only expense to which the government would be subjected would be the expense of furnishing the needed incentive in the shape of a bounty for every gallon of oil rendered or every fish caught. There is just one point to which I wish to call attention, and that is -with regard to the lobster fishing industry, and I refer to this because the commission has not yet finished its work. I .would call attention to it in particular to the operations along our coast. No doubt the investigations of the previous commission have been productive of the very greatest good, but there are certainly some defects in the conclusions at which they arrived. One of these defects is the great inequalities in the length of the season in different districts. I would therefore suggest that the commission pay particular attention to the equalizing of the lobster fishing season around the Island of Cape Breton. There is nearly a month's difference in the time within which fishermen can prosecute that industry in different parts of the coast around that island. I am sure the House will agree that a difference of three weeks in the open season in one locality is quite unrea sonable.
With regard to the proposition to establish factories for the manufacture of oil and other valuable products from the dogfish. I would again say that this- would be a very costly way of disposing of the fish, although it might be profitable in some localities. The great obstacle would be the difficulty of applying such a system along 5,000 miles of coast. From the southern side of the Bay of Fundy to Labrador there is a fishing coast of that length and to establish these factories would involve an immense expense. What is more, the fish is of a migratory character and when a factory had been built at great expense perhaps in three weeks after its completion this pest would migrate to another shore. I would therefore press upon the government the choice of giving a bounty per head for every dog-fish taken or else of so much a gallon for every gallon of oil extracted. In this way the whole coast would be covered much better than by experimenting in any one locality.

speechtext: Does my hon. friend think the fish could be used for food to any extent ?

I have never heard of it being used for food among our people.
(Mr. WADE. I believe that some have been canned.
.TTTT.Y 19. 1904
Mr. McLennan. Not that I have heard of. The oil is quite valuable, and as a fertilizer they are excellent. The farmers along out coast woukj lose no time I am sure in adopting them as a fertilizer and paying the fishermen for them. I make these observations on behalf of the fishermen along the 150 miles of coast in the county which I have the honour to represent. What holds true of that coast, no doubt holds true of several other constituencies in the province from which I come.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman if the dog-fish has ever been analysed so that we might be able to tell whether it is fit for food or only for manure ? Before we undertake to discuss the dog-fish, we should know its component parts, and what it is fit for. It has been discussed ever since we started this morning at 11 o'clock, but I have yet to learn what it is good for. It seems to be a great evil to the fishermen, and we should know what it is worth.
Dog-fish have been analysed and are found good as food. I think 90 per cent of the fish is good for food, and the bi-products form excellent fertilizers.

I was glad to bear the hon. member for West Elgin ask this [DOT]question, because I apprehend that this question should be discussed by the people of Ontario more than by the people of the maritime provinces. This is one of the vital questions of Canada. The fishery Interests of the maritime provinces are the mqst vital in Canada. They are infinitely superior to the wheat interests, the mineral interests or the agricultural interests of Canada. This matter should be taken up in the most liberal spirit so that the government if necessary may spend not only $100,000, but $1,000,000 to exterminate this pest. This is a new menace to the fishing interests in the maritime provinces. What we want is a commission that will summon to its aid the most scientific knowledge in the country to determine where these dogfish grow and then to ascertain the best and most effective means to secure their extermination, because exterminated they must be, otherwise they will destroy the fishing industries in Canada. They are the most important industries in the wolrld. Down by the seas you have a maritime and a commercial people. Without a maritime and commercial population this country would be inland, and inland countries have ever been failures. You must have a mercantile country. The men who control the sea, who go abroad, are the ones who determine the character of a country. You train these men in the fisherise of the maritime provinces, and if you want a navy
Oh, oh. .

I am surprised at the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Maepherson). Is he so narrow as to be absolutely unaware of the enormous proportions of the fishing industries of the maritime provinces ? The other matter is the commercial interest of this country, in which British Columbia ought to have some concern. I am surprised that hon. gentlemen should take so-little interest in this matter. I suppose if it had been a question that offered some-personal advantage to some one, they would have been on their feet. But apparently no subject that does not offer some personal reward to seme members of this House-appeals to their hearts or their statesmanship. I want the hon. gentleman to know that the fish industries of the maritime .provinces are among the most important industries in this country. The only things I regretted in the remarks of the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson)-who is generally liberal to a fault and sometimes conservative to a fault-was his remark that this discussion commenced at 11 o'clock and it was time to finish it. Why,, Sir, in the interests of Canada it should be continued for two months, if it were necessary. If it were some little vote of $2,000" for a wharf, then I suppose he would be willing to let it continue for a week. But when a vital interest is being discussed when the great fishing interests of this country are at stake, that is another thing.
Now I want to say that without great fishing interests you cannot have a commercial marine and you cannot have a navy. I want to see in a few years a navy, so that if my children desire to pursue a naval course they can do so on Canadian vessels instead of having to go abroad. I want to see a navy in this country. From what other source can you find men to man your navy unless from those who are engaged in the fishing industry ? Can you man vour navy with men from Ontario or from Manitoba ? Why, Sir, a ship manned by Manitobans or Ontarians would sink in half an hour. You want the men down by the sea to man your ships. Maritime people alone can produce a successful navy. These are the sailors that fight on the ships that win victories, it does not depend on the number of the ships or the tonnage of the navy. Now if we want a navy in this country we must encourage the great fishing interests of the maritime provinces. I say that if need came we could furnish in the maritime provinces 20,000 or 50,000 of the finest sailors in the world. Give them three months training on board a ship, and ihey would fight the fleets of Japan and Russia combined, and sink them. I want to see questions of this kind appeal to the manhood of Canada, and relegate little questions to county councils. This is a vtal question, and I ask the government to spare no pains in dealing with it. If it

takes $100,000, vote it; if it takes $1,000,000, vote it; vote all that is required to destroy the pest of the dog-fish. I have no technical knowledge of the fishing industries myself, I only know that with $1,000,000 you can get the technical information necessary to protect our fisheries. Therefore I would ask parliament to vote, if necessary, $1,000,000 to save the fishing interests of the maritime provinces, because they would serve for the foundation of a great commercial navy which I hope to see built up in this country.
I do not knew why the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Gourley) singled me out for some of his jibes.

I will tell you why. 1 noticed on one or two occasions while I was speaking-I do not know whether it is the training that British Columbia people receive or not, I am not familiar with their training-but I noticed that the hon. gentleman was acting in a very boisterous manner, wrhat I would call an ill-bred manner, in attempting interruptions.

Mr. Chairman, 1 think I am in the judgment of every member of the House if my conduct since I have been here does not at least stand a fair comparison with that of the hon. gentleman. I do not think I have ever got up in this House and rambled all over God's green earth in making a speech. If the hon. gentleman is annoyed because, in conversation with a gentleman at my right, who saidj something to me which caused me to laugh while the hon. gentleman was speaking. I am prepared to apologize fpr my laugh, though to tell the truth i was not laughing at anything the hon. gentleman said, because most of what he said was not worth laughing at. Even if I did wish to laugh at him while he was speaking, there is no law in this country to forbid me. I think my breeding is quite as good as his, and I thinks my conduct in this House will compare favourably with his own. I would not have spoken on this dog-fish question if the hon. member had not unnecessarily brought my name into the discussion, but we in the west have some interest in this particular question. But we have not come to parliament like the hon. member for Colchester asking the government to contribute $1,000,000 towards exterminating the pest. We have dog-fish on our coasts and have had for years, but we deal with the pest ourselves, instead of asking the government to interfere on our behalf in the exercise of paternalism. I am a Canadian first, last, and all the time, and I believe that what is good for Nova Scotia is good for British Columbia. We in British Columbia have settled the dogfish question some time ago. We have erected refineries there. We catch the fish Mr. GOURLEY.
and render them into oil and use the offal as a fertilizer. The result is that we have two companies there who are now making money out of it, and *ve do not come to the Dominion parliament asking for paternal assistance. I believe there is a little too much paternalism exercised by the government in behalf of people who expect government assistance for every little industry they start, or every little difficulty they get into. No doubt our people in British Columbia would be pleased if they could receive some benefit in the way of a bounty towards destroying the dog-fish pest. Our dog-fish are just as disastrous to other fish as they are down in the maritime provinces. The only difference is that our dog-fish do not go into the rivers in such large quantities, they stay in the open sea. Our salmon go into the fresh water, and when the dog-fish do not follow them into fresh water, but are caught in traps and by an apparatus made specially for the purpose, consisting of strong steel hooks which the fish cannot bite through.

speechtext: Are they put to any use in British Columbia ?

Yes. The oil is largely used as a lubricant, they call it skidway oil. We use a lot of it in our country in lumbering operations. That may seem strange to people in the east. But we have no snow there to facilitate the getting out of logs, and the people use skidways which they grease with this oil. Dog-fish livers make an oil equal to cod liver oil, and a good many people use it medicinally. I am aware from personal knowledge that it makes as good an oil as* cod liver oil. There is no better fertilizer than the residue from the refinery.

SIR ELZEAR TASCHEREAU AND LORD DUNDONALD,
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I wish to draw the attention of the government to a cablegram which appears in the evening papers- in the Evening ' Citizen ' of to-day and in the Ottawa Evening ' Journal.' The cablegram is to the same effect. That in the ' Citizen ' reads as follows :
London, July 19.-Sir BIzear Taschereau, chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, says he is indignant at the political capital being made out of the Dundonald affair. He says the London ' Times ' is being loaded up by Ottawa Tory

sources. There are few Scotchmen back of the whole agitation, and he cannot see how the British government, if alive to its own interests, can fail to recall Lord Dundonald before the end of the week.
In the ' Journal ' of this evening the cable is as follows :
London, July 19.-Sir Elzear Taschereau says he is indignant that political capital is being made of the Dundonald affair. The ' Times ' is loaded up by Ottawa Tory sources. Few Scotchmen back the whole agitation. He cannot see how British government, if alive to its own interests, can fail to recall Dundonald before the end of the week.
I can hardly believe it possible that these cables reflect accurately the views given in public by this distinguished jurist. His Lordship enjoys an enviable reputation as an impartial jurist, but if he desires to maintain that splendid position he must refrain from the public discussion of purely political matters. It is hardly in accord with the fitness of things that His Lordship -who is at present in London in attendance, upon the sessions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the Supreme Court of the empire-should make use of this language, or should give utterance to these views regarding a gallant British officer who is only defending himself against the unfair and unjustifiable attacks which have been made and are being made upon him. Lord Dundonald is no longer in the service of Canada. He no longer occupies the position of General Officer Commanding the Canadian militia, and if, as it is claimed by some hon. gentlemen, that, notwithstanding the fact that he occupies no official position in Canada or in connection with the Canadian government, although a distinguished officer of the British army, it is impolitic on his part to make public speeches or to discuss a matter of this kind in which he is so vitally interested, what shall be said of the course which is being pursued by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada in this connection ? I would like to ask the government if the statement I have read has been brought to its attention ; if this statement has been authorized : if the,government approves of it, and if it will make some definite announcement as to the position of the government, either now or at the sitting of the House to-morrow ?

speechtext: I would like to draw the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that these cables have come by our own special Canadian cable service that is paid for by the people of Canada, and they are likely to be official on that account. That is the reason why I think we are entitled to have some definite statement from the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wishes to imply that these cables are in any way under the control of the. government or that the government have anything to do with them he is certainly mistaken. We grant a sum of money to aid the Canadian Press Association in the dissemination of their news but they manage the matter entirely and I can assure my hon. friend that we have not really any more control over these cables than he himself. I do not wish to offer any opinion whatever concerning them.

subtopic: SIR ELZEAR TASCHEREAU AND LORD DUNDONALD,
speechtext: The hon. minister misapprehends what I meant to say. I meant to say that this cable service was supposed to devote most of its space to Canada. It was for that reason that the cable service was subsidized and for that reason I believe the service will be more likely to be official and accurate than an ordinary associated press cablegram might be expected to be.

speechtext: How much was surveyed last year ? The hon. gentleman told us last year that it was his intention to have 500 townships surveyed in the Northwest during this year. How many townships have been surveyed and where have, the surveys been made ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC-EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS ON SURVEYS.
speechtext:
I have a statement of the work done last year but have not got it under my hand. I shall lay it on the table to-morrow. The work for this year is as follows :
1.	Three parties under daily pay at $15,000 each-$45,000.
Three survey parties are to be kept at work for twelve months in the Peace River District, establishing base lines and block outlines, which are the governing lines of the system of survey of Dominion Lands. These lines have to be marked on the ground in order that subdivision surveys may be undertaken in the near future.
Each party is'in charge of a Dominion Land Surveyor whose salary is $7.50 per day. The assistant is paid $3 per day ; the the cook and labourers are hired at the current rate of wages of this district. A party consists of fourteen men besides the surveyor and the assistant. The cost is about $45 per day. "
2.	Three parties under daily pay at $10,000 each-$30,000.
Three parties are to be employed during the coming season in surveying base lines and block outlines west of Edmonton and from Lesser Slave lake westwards along the 19th base line. These parties will be of the same strength as those sent to Peace river.
3.	Five parties under daily pay at $7,500 each -$37,500.
For surveying the outlines of townships between the base lines before commencing the subdivision and for making subdivision and other surveys which cannot be executed under contract, it is proposed to have five parties. One is to work in Manitoba, one in Southern Alberta and three around Edmonton and at Athabaska Landing. An outline party consists of a surveyor in charge at $6.50 per day, an assistant at $3 per day, a cook and nine or ten labourers. The cook and labourers are engaged at the current rate of wages of the country in which they are working. The cost is from $30 to $35 per day.
4.	One party under daily pay at $17,000.
The surveys made more than twenty years ago were marked by wooden posts and mounds. The posts have been destroyed by prairie or bush fires and the mounds being more or less obliterated, new settlers have great difficulty in finding the limits of their lands. The lines of these old surveys are being gradually renewed and marked with iron posts. By taking the townships in large blocks and employing a numerically strong party, the work can be done for five to six dollars per mile, which is less than half the cost of the original subdivision. It is proposed to renew the marks of survey in a block of fifty-one townships near Touchwood Hills, In eight townships at Willow Bunch in Southern Assiniboia and six townships near Prince Albert, or in sixty-five townships altogether. The work Is to be done by one party consisting of a surveyor at $7.50 per day, four assistants at $3 each, twenty-nine labourers and a cook at current wages. The cost is estimated at $75 per day.
5.	Three parties under daily pay at $7,500 each-$22,500.
For restoring the marks of obliterated surveys in Manitoba and near Edmonton, two parties are to be employed. Another party is to retrace the lines of townships in Manitoba which were badly surveyed. The lines will not be changed but plans will be made showing

their directions and lengths and the actual contents of every quarter section. The parties will be of the same strength as those employed for the survey of township outlines.
6.	Two parties under daily pay at $8,000 each -$16,000.
The surveys in the British Columbia Railway Belt are made by two parties, one attending to the eastern part of the belt and the other one to the western part. The parties are of the same strength as those employed for the survey of township outlines The cost per day Is a little more than in the Northwest Territories om account of the higher wages of labourers.
7.	One party under daily pay at $6,000.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC-EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS ON SURVEYS.
speechtext:
Wheeler completed last year his survey of the Selkirk range in the vicinity of the Canadian Pacific Railway. His report and map are being published and will prove of great interest and value to the constantly increasing number of persons who are visiting the mountains every summer. He is now to commence the survey of the Rocky Mountains between the Gap and the Columbia river and to prepare a report descriptive of the country. His salary is $2,000 a year ; he has two assistants at $75 and $60 a month respectively and during the summer engages a few labourers for work on the ground. His office is at Calgary, Alta.
8.	One party under daily pay at $5,000. It is proposed to have an exploration made of the Peace River District for the purpose of ascertaining where the best lands for settlement are situated. After these lands are located, steps will be taken for their subdivision at an early date. Incidentally, information will be collected to assist In selecting the 3,500,000 acres in the Peace River country which the province of British Columbia has agreed to convey to the Dominion. The party is to be in charge of Mr. Thos. Turnbull and will consist only of a few labourers. Mr. Turnbull's salary Is $2,000 a year.
9.	Four parties under dally pay at $6,800 each-$24,000.
The subdivision of townships into sections being executed under contract, it is necessary to have a thorough inspection made In order td make sure that the surveys have been properly and accurately executed and that the charges for doing the work are in accordance with the terms of the contract. Four Dominion Land Surveyors will be employed as inspectors ; each will have1 a party consisting of six labourers and a cook. The salary of the inspectors is $6.50 per day and the cost of each party is estimated at $25 per day.
10.	Fifty subdivision survey contracts at $7,600 each-$380,000.
The Dominion Lauds Act provides that except In special cases the township subdivision surveys of Dominion Lands shall he performed under contract at a certain rate per township, per mile, or per acre, fixed from time to time by the Governor in Council or by competitive tender. The present rate has been fixed by the Governor in Council and varies according to the difficulty of the work, from $7 per mile in bare prairie to $30 and $35 per mile in the woods. The subdivision of a township (not including the exterior boundaries laid out by surveyors under daily pay) requires the survey of forty-eight miles of section lines and of the lakes and rivers within the township. The cost varies from $350 in the hare prairie to $2,000 and over In the woods. A full township provides sixty-four free homesteads.

The surveys contemplated for the coming season comprise four hundred townships, the bulk of the work being situated west of the South Saskatchewan and south of Battleford, where a block of one hundred and eighty-three townships, mostly prairie, is to be subdivided The location of the townships is as follows :-

11.	Irrigation surveys, $13,000.
The irrigation surveys and the administration of the Irrigation Act are under the supervision of the Commissioner of Public Works of the Northwest Territories. The work includes the measurement of the discharge of streams and a topographical survey of the country suitable for irrigation, with a view to the best utilization of the quantity of water available. Two or three survey parties have been engaged on this work for several years and a number of observers are employed at various points on the streams. The work is to be continued as before at an established cost of $13,000
12.	Yukon survev office, $40,000.
13.	Employees at Ottawa, $90,000.
The greater part of the surveys staff consists of temporary clerks paid out of the appropriation for Dominion land surveys. There are at present ninety-seven, persons thus employed. They have to examine, plot and prepare for publication, the surveys made by surveyors in r.he field and to attend to the miscellaneous work incidental to a large survey office.
The plans of townships subdivided and of other surveys are lithographed for departmental use, for distribution to agents and for safle to the public. The lithographic office, where the work is done, consists of nine employees and costs about $4,800.
In the photographic office, plans are copied, enlarged or reduced as needed and plates for photozinography prepared. The office consists of six employees and costs about $3,040.
14.	20,000 iron posts, $5,000.
The corners of townships and sections are marked with iron posts made of gas 'tubing. The price averages 25 cents each. 20,000 posts are needed for the coming season.
15.	Miscellaneous, $19,000.
This item is t* cover surveying instruments, printing and supplies of various kinds.
