speechtext: The reason I ask is that in one township, township No. 19, range 19, Which is in the permanent timber reserve there are many settlers who have petitioned the government to have it thrown open for settlement. There is practically no timber in the township and in view of the fact that land has been sold by the railway companies in that township, it seems to be the height of folly to retain it in the timber reserve. Either the settlers should be notified that it is to be kept as a timber reserve and no settlement permitted, or it should be thrown open for homesteading.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC-EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS ON SURVEYS.
speechtext: Are there a number of half-breeds in that township ?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC-EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS ON SURVEYS.
speechtext:
,T. ROCHE. Yes, it is near Clearwater lake.
Among papers which were brought down in answer to a motion by the bon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Stewart) I noticed some correspondence between the Dominion and provincial governments, sfhowing that the provincial government sold some land in this township, but it had not been surveyed by the Dominion government and the attention of the I[DOT]onlinion government was drawn to this. Again some railway companies have their lands situated in that township, and have been selling some of their lands to set-tiers. The township is practically without timber and the half-breeds who have settled in it are anxious to know whether they are to be permitted to remain there. Some of them have waited on me and asked me to bring the matter to the minister's attention. I forwarded several petitions, which _ I received, to the department asking that' these settlers be notified as soon as possible whether or not they are to be allowed to take np homesteads. I had a conversation with Crown Timber Inspector Stevenson, in Winnipeg last year and he said that legislation would be introduced this session in regard to that timber reserve. Is it the intention of the government to introduce such legislation or what decision has been come to in reference to this particular township.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC-EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS ON SURVEYS.
speechtext:
I have had the facts brought before me and1 have given them some consideration. As to the people being notified not to take up homesteads, I think my bon. friend will admit that they were perfectly well aware that this land is on a timber reserve, but my hon. friend will no doubt

figree that it is sometimes necessary to do more than give notice in order to keep people off government lauds. As to the colony in this particular township to whicu my hon. friend refers, some of the cases will be more or less difficult to deal with. It is not settled under the provision of the Dominion Lands Act at all. I have not been able to make up my mind positively as to how this township should be dealt with, but I think I have all the facts and only one point remains to be cleared up. I may say to my hon. friend that I think some land now in the reserve will have to be taken out of it before we make a final settlement of the question. One of the railway companies, I think it is the Canadian Northern Railway, have the right under the old Order in Council to select lands in that timber limit, but this railway was notified by the department some time ago that the department was willing to give them other lands in other places. The last communication which I saw on the subject was to the effect that their sales were not irrevocable and they were willing to carry out the suggestion as to the government acquiring these lands. We are considering the question now for the purpose of seeing what can be done. Of course the question of protecting a purchaser may arise. What I propose to do is to endeavour to effect an amicable and reasonable settlement all around so that I can introduce legislation which I would have introduced before tins if this question about the land sold by the railway company had not been brought up. When that is out of the way I shall introduce legislation to finally define the bounds of these .timber limits. As to the odd numbered sections, so far as the Canadian Northern is concerned, they have agreed to dispose to us of their sections in exchange for lands in other places and practically the only question which remains is whether there are any individual purchasers who have to be reckoned with. As to that we are now getting information.

speechtext: Petitions have been sent to the government for several years past in reference to this, and the invariable reply has been that the department intended to send out an inspector and that as soon as his report was received the government would act on his report. I understand that one officer was sent out there last winter, made an investigation and reported. I think liis name was Mr. Stewart.

township joined to the permanent timber reserve, or else that a certain reserve should be set apart for these half-breeds, giving them small limits inside of the township. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC-EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS ON SURVEYS.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows well, of course, that these people had no business to go there in t'he last two years as this is a permanent timber reserve. My hon. friend and I both know perfectly well that it is sometimes difficult to keep people off government reserves, especially if there is any timber on them, or in their neighbourhood. But what I want to say is this : We want first of all to get the reserves into the hands of the government. subtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC-EMPLOYMENT OF ALIENS ON SURVEYS.
speechtext: Mr. Speers reported last December and in persuing Mr. Speers' report one is struck with the fact that he does not say himself definitely that these settlers are really on the land. They have already secured 150,000 acres out of 250,000 acres which they are to get from the government on the strength of the number of homestead entries which they secure not on the strength of those who are absolutely on the land, because it has been charged through the public press that many of these are fictitious entries made by those who have no idea whatever of locating upon the land and I think it is a very poor criterion of actual settlement merely to take the recorded list of entries. But, already 150,000 acres of land have been handed over on the report of Mr. Speers, although that report does not say that these men are in actual occupation of the land. It simply goes on to say that so many homestead entries have been made and it is taken as evidence that the company have fulfilled that portion of their contract. I do not think that is fair or just. In support of the position which I take in regard to this matter I would read a letter that appeared last year in the Toronto ' Globe ' from a gentleman who has himself voluntarily homesteaded in that country. It is as follows :

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
'Homesteader,' Regina, writes :-We noticed an article in the ' Globe ' of July 10th referring to the abuse of homestead rights in northern Ontario in regard to the waste of timber. We have something going on here equally as bad. I have homesteaded on land seven miles from Regina and Prince Albert Railway. I made my entry in the last of September and went on my land in the beginning of May. I made my entry' here direct in the Dominion land office without the intervention of any land company, but I am in the midst of the Saskatchewan Valley Land Co.'s territory and have seen some of the methods of settlements going on. They agreed with the government to find twenty homesteaders in each township, in the choosing of lands this company has been given the privilege, hitherto not accorded to any company, of choosing what lands they please for sale, whether odd or even numbered sections and leaving for homesteaders what lands they please, whether even or odd. As a consequence all or,nearly all the homesteads are poor or almost worthless and the company has the best land for sale. As a result there is a great laxity in regard to homestead regulations. These poor homesteads are offered as an inducement by the company to intending purchasers and many buy on that understanding. Many of them never expect to live on them, hut to hold the homestead for a while and then sell out with the homestead

[DOT] 7033
thrown in as an inducement for purchasing. Those who have gone in on homesteads cannot tell what is homestead and what is sold and can get scant information, as the government land agents, at least the one I had to get my information from is a relative of the president, and consequently in sympathy with the said company and their purchasers. Where we are at present there are three of us who have started in actual residence of our homesteads, and for six miles around there are only three living on homesteads, yet there are many homesteads around us taken up as soon as ours and no one on them. We are almost alone and like Robinson Crusoe for loneliness, In the midst of a large tract of land held by land speculators. Nearly all has been sold or homesteaded around us, but now, more than nine months after entry, there is nothing doing and no one on these homesteads held by the speculators waiting for the rise in the price of land. We think the department at Ottawa did a very unwise thing in allowing this company to make odd numbered section homesteads. If there were a uniform system as to what was homestead and what land company land, we poor homesteaders could see that these absentee homesteaders had their claims cancelled, but we can not get any but scant information as to what is not homestead. An American can secure favours with this company that an native Canadian cannot enjoy. We know of cases where men had made excuses to the land agent and they do not intend to come on their homesteads until next spring. They just came in and promised to have five acres broken and then went away to Minnesota again. We think this is an unjust stretching of the rules and regulations in regard to homestead regulations and very unfair with those who are complying with them. We are of the opinion that the ways and methods of this land company need to be investigated, as the way in which homestead regulations are violated is the laughing-stock of those who are on homesteads and by none more than Americans who have taken homesteads. They think we must have a very strange government that will allow any company to do as has been done by the Saskatchewan Valley Land Co. I may say that what I am speaking of takes place a little over a hundred miles north-west of Regina.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What is the date of that letter ?

It is from the ' Globe of the 1st of August, 1993. Apparently this gentleman is not an opponent of the government ; at any rate, he is a devoted reader of the Toronto ' Globe,' and he sent his communication to it. I happened to see this letter last fall, and I thought it only proper to bring it to the attention of the minister because if these charges are true they are very serious, and they show" that my contention is strictly correct ; that these gentlemen come in. take up homesteads, purchase a certain amount of land at as low a rate as possible from the company ; wait until the price increases ; sell it; pocket their profit, and throw their homestead in, which may be of inferior land.
What is the name of the writer of that letter ?
I said he signed it ' Homesteader.'
Oh ; it is an anonymous letter.

I presume the Toronto [DOT] Globe ' has the writer's name, and if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) desires to get it he will probably receive it from his friends of the ' Globe ' much readier than I could.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was asked before six o'clock as to the conditions of sale by the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. It is evident that the person who wrote letter read by my hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) was under a misapprehension with regard to some points. His statement with regard to the homesteading of odd numbered sections is made in entire misapprehension of the facts, because there has been no homesteading of the odd numbered sections in that tract at all. The odd numbered sections were reserved long years ago for the land grant to the Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, and the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company having purchased the land grant of that railway had the right to select the land from these odd numbered sections. We do not deal with the odd numbered sections at all ; our dealing was altogether with the even numbered sections. As to the question of the settlement being bona fide or not, the settlers make their settlement in accordance with the ordinary rules. Every settler has to make his affidavit in the regular form, stating that he is bona fide taking up his land for his own benefit alone, and that he intends to reside and make his home upon it. Under the law he has six months to go upon it and reside, and an extension of time may be given. I do not remember whether there were any extensions of time in this particular tract or not, but the number of extensions is comparatively small, and the extensions have been given on what seemed to be reasonable ex cuses. That which is referred to by the correspondent as indicating bad faith is no indication of bad faith at all. He says a number of people went there and took up their homestead entries and went back to the States. Well, that is what a great many settlers from the United States do. They take up the lands and go back for their families, as most of them do not bring their families in until the next year. However, before they get the land they have to fulfil the settlement duties. So far as this particular tract is concerned, some time an order was given to the homestead inspector to make a thorough inspection of the whole tract. Patents were granted by officers of the department to the extent of



something like 150,000 acres. There was deposited $50,000 on account of the balance of the land, and we shall have the report of the homestead inspector as to the exact performance of the settlers' duties. I do not think there is any fear that the transactions will not be carried out.

The gravamen of the charges made in that letter, and what I intended to convey was that the government had disposed of 150,000 acres already on the strength of the homestead entries, and that there was no read proof that settlement had taken place. The minister does not attempt to contravene that statement. On the strength of Mr. Speers' report he has handed over
150,000	acres out of the 250,000 acres, and Mr. Speers does not attempt to prove that these settlers are actually on the land. That they have taken the homestead entries is an evidence of good faith that these settlers are on the land, but as a matter of fact they are not. Notwithstanding that after the homestead entry has been made, six months is given to them to go on the land, the gentleman who wrote this letter has distinctly stated that nine months have elapsed and practically none of them were on the land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will not assume that the statements in this letter are to be taken literally, because on the face of it the writer shows that he does not know the facts when he says the odd numbered sections are being homesteaded.

That is a technical point which the minister takes advantage cf. This gentleman may not be aware that they purchased the odd numbered sections from the Regina and Long Lake Railway Company, but in other respects the writer shows that he is well acquainted with local conditions. He tells us that in a radius of six miles there are only six settlers, and he shows that he understands what he is talking about. He gives evidence that home stead entries have not been followed up by actual settlement. What we complain of is that 150,000 acres of this land grant is practically handed over to the company without satisfactory evidence that the settlers have been secured to the country. This government has stated that they have reversed the policy of their predecessors and reserved the land for the settlers, but we charge that they have practically done nothing of the kind. The government has sold this land for $1 an acre ; the land may not have been worth very much when they sold it, but according to Mr. Speers' report some of the poorest of that land has been sold for $5 an acre by that company, and it sells up as high as $10 an acre. Another feature is that the government is taking scrip as well as cash in payment. In other words, instead of having $150,000 in cash for the 150,000 acres, Mr. Speers reports that they have scrip to the amount of $98,000 and cash to the amount of $52,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In my opinion scrip was never intended to be utilized' for the payment of lands in blocks such as this contract called for ; and I do not think it is right or proper for the government to practically assist any band of speculators, who no doubt purchased this script at a very reduced figure, possibly at 50 cents on the dollar or less to make large protits by accepting it at par. I see that there is a stipulation in the contract that ' they can pay in scrip or in cash. That feature of the contract I condemn. I think the government, when disposing of the lands so cheaply, should have insisted on being paid in cash and not in scrip. I also desire to point out that in the agreement entered with these gentlemen, there are the names of two Canadians, Mr. Macdonuell and Mr. Adamson. Mr. Macdonuell, I understand, 's the leader of the opposition in the territorial assembly. Mr. Adamson is the Liberal candidate in one of the constituencies for a seat in this House. I think it is not according to strict propriety that Mr. Adamson should be in that position and at the same time connected with such a large laud speculation. The hon. minister can see how he could use his position in many ways to bring pressure to bear on settlers who have taken up land, in order to secure their support. I think strict propriety should induce the government to advise Mr. Adamson either to retire from the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company or from his candidature for the Dominion House. I think the hon. minister himself will scarcely defend Mr. Adamson's position. I desire to ask the minister also, is it or is it not a fact that Mr. Turiff has some connection with the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company ? I have heard not only from his political opponents, but from many of his political supporters that Mr. Turiff is secretly connected with that company. In fact, they have intimated to me that he was compelled, through fear of his connection with it being disclosed, to resign his position of Dominion Land Commissioner. He also is a Liberal candidate for the representation of Eastern Assiniboia in this House, and he can use his position to influence the electors in the same was as Mr. Adamson. The minister will know whether that statement in regard to Mr. Turiff is true or not. If it is, he should not be allowed to occupy the position he does in connection with the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company and at the same time be a Liberal candidate for this House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
With regard to the contract, I may say that the number of settlers in the district was given in the report of the land agent last December, and upon that the officers of the department acted. The only question can be whether the settlers wiil remain on the land. Instructions have been issued to an inspector to go there for the purpose of verifying the fact. I

have not the slightest fear that the conditions regarding settlement will not be carried out. As to the price paid for the lands, all I can say is that these lands would have been homestead lands if we had not disposed of them in this way. Had settlers gone upon them, they would have returned no funds to the government. By the sale the lands returned to the government $1 an acre, so that, so far as money is concerned, the government is $250,000 ahead. The lands were surveyed sixteen or seventeen years ago, but settlers had passed through them and had gone to various other parts of the country. My information is that there were only three or four homestead entries in good standing in the department at the time the lands were disposed of. At the present time we have the prospect of a well-settled territory as a result of the arrangement made. As to the payment of scrip, it makes no difference in the world to the government whether the land is paid for in money or in scrip. Scrip is receivable in payment for Dominion lands, and sooner or later the government has to redeem it. As to Mr. Adamson's connection with the company, all I have to say is this, that we do not exercise any control over the electors of Humboldt. They have a right to nominate any one they like for a seat in this House, and they nominated Mr. Adamson. As to Mr. Turiff being connected with this contract. I never heard any rumour to that effect until something was said about it in one of the committees of the House. I believe Mr. Turiff was asked if he had any connection with the company, and he said he had not. That is all I know about it. When the rumour came to my knowledge, I asked him if he had any connection with the company, and he said he had not. It had nothing to do with his resignation of the position of Commissioner of Doriiinion Lands. Mr. Turiff had nothing whatever to do with the contract. It was made with the president of the company, Colonel Davidson, who discussed the matter with the deputy minister. My deputy informs me that various members of the company- were here, and that he discussed the matter with them. I never discussed it with them or saw any of them in connection with it. The question was submitted to me by the deputy minister, and I approved of it. So far as Mr. Turiff is concerned, he had nothing to do with and gave no advice in connnection with this matter, and I am informed that it was never brought before him. As to the general features of the transaction, the operations of the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, resulting from the acquisition of this tract of land, have been of immense benefit to the Northwest. If we had given the land to it for nothing, we would have received benefits ten times over in return. This company has been exceedingly efficient as a 224j
colonization agent. It has placed a lot of valuable settlers not only on this tract but on the remainder of its tracts. I can recall no feature of our colonization policy in the Northwest which has been attended with greater success than the efforts of this company. Every one familiar with the district will bear me out in what I say, that on this land, which was tenantless for many years, we have at the present time a very large and thriving settlement, which bids fair to grow not only in numbers, but in wealth.
I think the transaction is in every way advantageous to the country and one which will promote good settlement.

The minister has stated that settlers would not go into that country in years gone by, which is very true. Many years ago the land in that particular district was not looked upon as being very superior land and was not taken up as there were hundreds of thousands of acres of much better land available. But, as occurs in many countries, land is now being settled upon and purchased in Canada that would not have been taken up a few years ago. The minister states that an inspection of those lands will be made and that actual settlers will have to be provided for before the balance of the land will be handed over to the company. That is all very well after 150,000 acres out of the 250,000 have been handed over to them upon the mere strength of the homestead entries. I think it is a distinct admission by the minister that he has been rather remiss in this mattei-, and has been late in taking the stand he now proposes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the matter had been brought to my attention when the report was brought in, I would have given instructions that a special report should be made. As soon as it was brought to my attention I gave instructions for a special report.

ROiCHE. The minister was rather tardy in giving instructions, because-it is well known that 150,000 of the 250,000 acres have come into possession of the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company without sufficient proof being furnished for members of this House to see that the conditions of their contract have been complied with. In fact, I think when the discussion was up last session the minister himself remarked that they were not likely to fulfil their conditions, that is the condition that they were to have two-fifths of their settlers in these townships inside of two years. The minister then said :
The two years are not yet up, hut will be in a few months. It is very doubtful if they will be in a position to get anything.
That was in July last, but 150,000 acres of these lands have been handed over on the ground that the company have complied with the conditions, that is that thirty-two 1 settlers have been provided for each town-

ship. As a matter of fact, they have taken the report of Mr. Speers of the number of entries as proof in that regard. I wish to draw attention to this fact, that in order to arrive at that conclusion they had to group the townships. I ask the minister if that was the intention in the first place ? Had (hey not to take the townships separately, and did not this condition apply to each individual township rather than to a group of townships, for which an average would be struck ? I understand, according to the report of Mr. iSpeers, that the latter procedure has been followed ; whereas, as a matter of fact, the agreement and the intention of the agreement was that they were to secure thirty-two settlers in each individual township.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As to the last question which my hon. friend has raised, I may say that where they take any land they will have to take the whole township, and will have to have an average of so many for the whole township. They cannot scatter their settlement.

I think that no one in this House is as well acquainted with this tract of country as I am, because ever since the rail way was built through that section I have been travelling up and down it, that is for the last thirteen or fourteen years. To my mind, the bargain that has been discussed this evening is a first-class bargain tor the people of this country. For thirteen years there was not a settler in that district, not a homestead was taken except three or four, where some section foremen made some homestead entries. No one would go in, and I may say that if the whole tract had been offered to me previous to this arrangement with the government, simply on condition that I should pay the taxes, I would not have felt justified in taking it. What are the facts of the ease ? This com-.pany has spent a lot of money. All is not gold that glitters. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) talks about their getting the land so cheap. He forgets to take into consideration the vast amount of money that they have spent in advertising, not only that tract of country, but the whole Northwest. If we could trace it up, I fancy that a great deal of the immigration we are now getting should be attributed to the advertisements of these people in the United States. I have been in some of the large cities of the United States and have seen what this company have been doing. They took up a special train of ten or fifteen pullmans loaded with people from the western states, senators. &c., to show them what that country was like, and that train must have cost them a great deal of money. They took that land when there was no one upon it, and now the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) tries to make out that this land has been granted to them on homestead entries, but that the people are not there. The people must be there, for Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
there are large towns all along that line, which have sprung up since that company undertook the work of filling that country. There are large towns, large lumber yards and machine factories, dozens of stores, &c. If there was not some one back in the country these people would not be doing business, and if my hon. friend would take the trouble to go up the line of the Qu'Appelle and Long Lake Company, he would find that a large number of people have gone in there. Even the gentleman who wrote that letter would not have been there if it had not been for the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. He was in the west for thirteen years and never thought of going into that district until the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company began operations there. Then he went there and thought they had a good thing. Like many other people, he thought that all was gold that glittered. He, too, neglected to consider that this company have spent an enormous sum of money in advertising that country and advertising the whole Dominion. When the whole transaction is threshed out, I venture to say that the company will make very little money out of it. My hon. friend alluded to the fact that Mr. Adamson was a member of that company when it was formed some three or four years ago and the purchase was made, and he seemed to think that for that reason Mr. Adamson had no right to be a candidate. I have never before heard such a doctrine as that. Because a gentleman four or five years ago happened to have transactions with the government it is contended that he cannot now become a candidate if the people want him to run. The people of this country have not shut out Canadian Pacific Railway directors, for instance. If that rule had been enforced, many of those who occupied seats on this side of the House previous to 1896 could not have been members, because if you traced up their records you would find that a majority of them had acquired timber limits or had some such dealings with the government of the day. It is ridiculous to talk about such a doctrine. This gentleman went in there two years ago, and if the people of Humboldt want him-as they have shown by their large vote in his favour at the convention that they do want him-they will elect him by a large majority, and I think they have a perfect right to do so. The bargain, taking it all around, is one of the best bargains ever made for this country. It has already done a great deal for the western country, not only by the filling up of the regions which were always in the past looked upon as useless, but by filling up other sections of the country, because this company has spent thousands and thousands of dollars in advertising this country. This company have carried on their operations in a very businesslike way. The first thing they did on the prairie was to survey a town. Then they built large hotels with their own money, built livery barns and appointed men to show settlers over the country in order that they might select lands. They ran the hotels free. People came in under these circumstances, and now my tion. friend asks : Is it certain that the people on the land were brought in by that company ? Considering that the land lay there for thirteen years without any person going on it, we must assume that any one who is on the land there must have gone on it, directly or indirectly, through the efforts of the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company.

The hon. gentleman has made just such a defence as one would expect. He tells us this is a good bargain.
I do not know whether he is interested, but no one would be astonished if he furnished a portion of the scrip.

This has gone so far that not only from speakers on the other side but also from the Conservative press in this country comes the charge that I am a scrip speculator. That was stated in an article in the ' Mail and Empire ' the other day ; and although I do not take much stock in what appears in that paper, yet as this charge is repeated so often, I wish to state now that out of the thousands and thousands of scrip issued in the Northwest Territories at the time, I did not buy more than fifteen in all, and I bought that to put on some lands of my own.

Of course I must accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but his defence is not quite what it was on the last occasion. On the lasLoccasion his defence was that he had paid just as much as other people did for the scrip. Now it appears to be that he only bought a very limited quantity. However that is unimportant one way or" the other. One thing perfectly clear is that the contract has been utterly disregarded in every feature. We have the declaration of the hon. minister himself, copied in the report of Mr. Speers, that there is nothing more to show than that entries were made there, without a particle of proof that there was a single settler. I do not say that there are no settlers. Perhaps there are, but there are no pretense that the company fulfilled the contract, and that is the difficulty. I understood the hon. gentleman to say* that his attention was called to that after the grant of 150,000 acres had been made. I would like to ask him if he was aware at the time the 150,000 acres were granted this company that he only was in possession of a report stating that so many entries had been made and not stating what settlers were upon the land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I was not aware until after the grant was patented. When it was brought to my attention I gave instructions that an actual inspection should be made. My hon. friend must understand that a matter of that kind might go a certain distance without being brought to my attention. As soon as it was brought to my at. tention, I gave instructions to have an actual inspection made and also calling attention to the provisions of the contract.

I quite understand that small transactions might slip through, but am unable to understand how the officers of his department could take upon themselves to grant 150,000 acres of land without the authority to do so. Who took upon themselves to carry out a large transaction of the kind upon the report then given ? Who was the guilty party ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My deputy in the patent branch issued the patent. When the thing came to his knowledge he brought it to my attention. We discussed the terms of the contract and I gave my instructions.

The hon. minister knows that the contract was before his officers. It provides as follows :
It is agreed that the purchasers shall place twenty settlers on each free homestead land in each 'township and twelve on lands which may be sold by the purchasers, before they shall be entitled to the remaining even numbered sections. In other words, there shall be in each township twenty quarter-sections to he settled on by homesteaders and twelve on the company's sections which the settler may purchase.
That contract was in the minister's department, and some person in the department must have taken upon himself great responsibility. Surely the hon. gentleman has no officer in his department who would attempt to issue a patent for 150,000 acres of land upon the report of Mr. Speers which disclosed nothing that entitled the company to the lands. He cannot pass that over by saying that some one unknown to him had committed an act of that kind. Was it done on the recommendation of his deputy.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
If the deputy did not recommend it, who did ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We will make a careful search and find out exactly liow the transaction took place. My hon. friend must understand that there have been placed on these lands an average of twenty-one set-lers in each township where the company are operating.
That is not disclosed in the report.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As to whether the settlers have actually remained there or not, we have sent out our inspectors to find out. As the fulfilment of the remainder of the conditions, we have the deposit of $50,000 and the remainder of the 100,000 acres which the company will not willingly give up without trying to earn it. True the land has increased in value, but it is through the efforts of the company, and I have not the

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: the slightest doubt that, under present conditions, they will go on and earn that land. A year ago I had doubts, because at that time they had not been successful, but at present I have not the slightest doubt, and no doubt the report will show that all those settlers are there. The government has perfect security.

I have not talked about security. That is another branch which we may discuss later on. I have not stated what security the government has for the carrying out of the contract. I am calling attention particularly to the gross , irregularity, I may say the criminal conduct of an official in his department, with a contract of that description before his eyes, when it is disowned by the minister himself, denied by his deputy, and still neither of these gentlemen knows who is the guilty party. It is the most extraordinary statement I ever heard made in the House of Commons-that 150,000 acres of land is handed over to this company. Why, Sir, what conclusion will the country draw from that circumstances ? Either that the officers in his own department must be concerned in it, or they would never have taken upon themselves to be guilty of a transaction of that kind. Yet we are told by the minister that there is no impropriety in Mr. Adamson becoming a candidate-a candidate in support of the hon. gentleman himself, a candidate in his interest, a candidate that has been a participant in that transaction, a candidate to whom 150,000 acres of land was handed over. Will any person say there is no impropriety in that? It is a transaction that seems perfectly plain to be a conspiracy against the interest of the people. It is idle for the hon. gentleman to talk about the security. If there is any security it is not because he carried out the conditions of the contract, or that he was careful that his officers observed their duties. If he has security, it has been given in utter disregard of that sort of thing. Now I leave the hon. gentleman to stand convicted of a transaction in his department that shows the loosest kind of administration of the business of the people of this country. The department must have fixed designs upon the people of this country to have evaded the instructions and to hand these lands over to these persons who were not entitled, according to any information in the department, to a single acre. The hon. gentleman, only two or three months before, declared that so far as he knew then he did not think they were entitled to an acre of that land. I do not think the hon. gentleman is in a very enviable position. He had better hunt up the culprit in his department and dismiss him.
The hon. ministei and the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) have spoken about this land as bav-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: ing become valuable simply because it passed into the possesison of the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. For thirteen years nobody would settle on it, the hon. member himself would not have taken it for the taxes. Settlers passed by it and went into a more productive portion of the country because this was worthless. But as soon as the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company got possession of it, does he mean to say that the quality of the land improved so much simply because it changed owners ? It is true that these gentlemen advertised extensively, and how did they advertise ? In a manner that commends itself to the minister? I do not think so. The minister rather repudiated them last year. If it is true that these were worthless lands that nobody would settle on for thirteen years, they were no use, what did the Saskatchewan Land Company do ? They issued a prospectus lauding those lands to the skies as being amongst the most productive in the Northwest Territories. This was brought to the attention of the minister last session by the leader of the opposition :

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand that the company has issued a prospectus in which these lands were described in very glowing terms.

I am not responsible for the advertisements of lend companies.
The minister was quite unwilling that the land company should advertise these as being among the most productive lands in the Northwest Territories, because it would induce settlers to come in under false pretenses. If they are as good as described by the member for Saskatchewan, I do not think the members of this company need to be commiserated because of their bargain with this government. Take the 150,000 acres of which they have already secured possession, and which they have got at $1 an acre. In reality they have not paid $1 an acre, they paid $98,000 altogether in script, which they may have purchased for fifty cents on the dollar. But assuming that they paid in cash $1 an acre, or $150,000 they have sold that land, putting it at a low average, for $5 an acre. Mr. Speers in his report states that most of the land has been selling at $5 an acre. As a matter of fact it has sold from $5 to $10. But putting it at the lower figure, $5 an acre, they received $750,000. Deducting all expenses in connection with the transaction I think you will find that they have made $000,000 profit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman tries to make the point that the lands were sold at an undervaluation. There was a tract of
3.500.000	acres of land set apart from which the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company might select about
500.000	acres. That arrangement was made

many years ago before I took office. Matters progressed until I bad been in office for a year or two, and the company alleged that they were unable to earn 800,000 acres of land in the 3,500,000. This 3,500,000 was examined and reported upon by officers of the railway company and by officers of the government, and by far the greater portion of it was classified by them as being actually worthless, unfit for settlement, of such a character that the company could not recoup themselves out of it. So bad was it that this railway company brought an action in the Exchequer Court of Canada for the purpose of compelling the government to make good the contract, and to give them the equivalent of the 800,000 acres. We gave them 3,500,000 to select from, and they brought action in the Court of Exchequer for the purpose of proving that there was not 800,000 acres in that whole tract fairly fit for settlement. This particular tract that we are Talking about is the worst of the 3,500.000 acres. It was considered absolutely hopeless in every possible way. Within a year before this transaction took place, the solicitor of that railway company came to my office and asked me if I would favour securing from the government of Canada authority to pay them $1.25 an acre instead of giving them the 800,000 acres they were entitled to. That is to say, although they had 3,-
500,000	acres to select from, they wished me to make an offer, which they would accept, to settle with the company by paying them at the rate of $1.25 an acre for the whole
800,000	acres. This 250,000 acres was in the worst district and sold at $1 an acre a few months afterwards to these people with the settlement conditions to which I have referred and which are set out in the contract. Let me point out further that in the next season this land presented a little more favourable appearance. I am not alluding particularly to this tract, but to the whole 3,500,000 acres. The same people who bought the 250,000 acres went to the people who owned the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan land grant of 800,000 acres, and bought their entire land grant which they could select from this 3,500.000 without any settlement conditions. They bought the whole 800,000 acres from shrewd speculators like the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) who I believe was interested in the transaction ; they bought the whole 800,000 acres I think for $1.75 an acre, with the privilege of selecting it from the 3,500,000 without any conditons whatever. There could be no more absolutely conclusive evidence of the fact that the dollar an acre we got was the full value of the land without any settlement conditions whatever. If we had sold it for a dollar an acre without any settlement conditions we should have made a very good bargain.

In referring to the hon. gentleman's remarks last year as to the number of settlers sent in by the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, I find that the hon. gentleman said :
Of course they -have sent in a considerable number. I recollect now they applied to get some patents, and they filed some information with regard to settlers. But the evidence which they filed did not prove that they had complied with the conditions and consequently we did not give them the land.
Will the hon. minister explain what evidence the land company filed with the government in order to claim the patents for their land ? Was it homestead entries ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I presume they referred to homestead entries as sufficient evidence.
I was not willing to act upon that, hut subsequently the officers issued the patents on Mr. McCannel's report.

That is the ground , upon which we are condemning the bon. gentleman. It seems that last year the company had made application on the strength of homestead entries to get their land. The hon. minister refused and notwithstanding that refusal the land has been banded over to them on the strength of that evidence.

I wish to say that the explanation in regard to the land seems rather strange in view of the fact that when you look over the surveyors' field-notes you find that land is graded No. 1, No. 2, 'No. 3 and No. 4. Quite a portion of this land is graded No. 2 and No. 3. Under those circumstances it could not have been such very bad land, because No. 2 and No. 3 would be fairly average good land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This land is hi the worst tract of the whole lot.
These are your own Surveyors' field-notes as to quality.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has been examined by expert land examiners on behalf of the railway companies and on behalf of our department and so far as this particular tract of land is concerned we have their statement that it was no good, that it was absolutely worthless.

Is the examination of your surveyors of no value ? It has always been regarded as of value. For the last twenty years or more we have been getting that information and settlers have accepted it as evidence of the quality of land. If land is graded as No. 1 it is regarded as the best land, if No. 2 It is fairly good land, and if No. 3 it is fairly good land, and if No. 4 it is regarded as not being very good land. The value which was attached to it twenty years ago has

been accepted. Whatever means the surveyors took of satisfying themselves of the quality of the land, I presume that the land is the same as it was before.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not the statement Of the expert examiners.

The expert examiner is not likeiy to go over it as carefully as the surveyor did, because the surveyor has to run up both sides of each section and he makes his report upon it. The land examiners are not likely to go over the lots as carefully as the surveyor is required to do.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what they were sent there for.
I do not think the inspectors go over every foot of land when they go into a locality to ascertain what is the general quality of the land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This matter was a sore subject with the department, a subject of dispute, a subject that became so acute that the railway company finally sued us for damages in the Court of Exchequer. They claimed that they should select the land farther north. They did not claim that they ought to have taken this land.

_Wliat portion is good land and what portion is bad land, because what I saw of it did not lead me to the impression that it was bad land ? There is another thing which seems to strengthen me in the impression that it is not bad land and it is the fact that it has been sold to farmers who have gone and examined it for themselves and who ought to be good judges. It has been sold to them for $5, $7 and $8 an acre. That does seem to be conclusive evidence that the land could not be so very bad.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I hope it will turn out better than we expected.

Before this arrangement was made you could not get any person to look at the land at all. A very strong corporation, the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company were using every means even going so far as to go to tile courts to prove that the whole district was absoluteiy worthless and for years every effort proved entirely unavailing to get any person to get off the train and examine the land.
They have read the speeches of some of your friends.

The bon. gentleman if he knows anything, knows that one reason was because there were a few dry years in that country it led to the impression that the land was in the dry belt and was of practically no value for farming purposes. The result was that a good many people

who had settled on that land during the dry years got up -and left it because of the feeling which they had that they could not carry on agricultural pursuits successfully. But this same district to-day seems to be as fine as any other district in the Northwest Territories.

Very likely this district will prove so, but what I have stated is the absolute fact that no person could be got to get off the train to look at this territory. For a hundred miles through this territory where there had been a railway in operation since 1890 only three homestead entries had been recorded. Between Lumsden, twenty miles north of Regina, and Saskatoon, on the south branch of the Saskatchewan river, a distance of over 100 miles, except one little ranching community at Dundurn, although a railway had been running through that country for twelve of thirteen years, there was not a single farmer, not one single settler, and people could not even be prevailed upon to look at the land partly as a result of the action of the railway company which had gone to the length of going to the courts to prove that the district was absolutely worthless.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is in possession of the facts, or whether he has ever been there or not. But, we have to accept his statement that there is only one farmer in that district. My information is a little different, but we have to accept his statement and take it for granted that he knows. I would only remind him that the Calgary ana Edmonton Railway runs through a section of the country that is regarded to-day as one of the most valuable in the Northwest Territories and that a few years ago you could go northward for 100 miles from Calgary and find very little land settled. Up to the last few years you could go to many of these stations and right up to The railway you would find no land settled. That railway was in existence for settlers and running all right. The real cause was that there was plenty of other land available for settlement and that a few dry seasons frightened the people out of that country. I know many who left that district believing it was not likely to be fit for agriculture, but I take it that the reports of the surveyors are as good evidence as we can have of the quality of the land, and they grade it into two or three classes.

The very same people compose the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company and the Calgary and Edmonton Land Company, as are interested in these lands, and they made no objection against accepting the lands along the line of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway. The conditions along that line were quite different.

The southern portion of the Calgary anti Edmonton Railway is through range country where until recent years there were not many homestead entries made.
Why were there no homestead entries made when there was a railway there ?

North of Calgary for a distance of perhaps fifty miles, similar cm-ditions prevail to those prevailing south of Calgary to the American boundary line. It is range country and until recent years there were ranches and ranching towns every few miles along the line, but there were not many homesteads. On the Prince Albert Branch Railway north of Regina, when you got north of the town of Lumsden you ran for more than a hundred miles without seeing a single individual except a few section lhen in summer and even they were not there in the winter time. Let me say to the House that if it had not been for this arrangement made with these American land speculators, these enterprising people, I venture to say the railway of the hon. gentleman's friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) would be out of commission to-day, and they would not be running trains over it. On the 11th of February last year, I was on a train on that line which wandered off upon the prairie. I do not think it was running at a greater speed than ten miles per hour, but the ties were so rotten that even with the aid of the winter frost they were unable to hold the rails to keep the train upon the right of way. Until this arrangement was made two years ago, there was so little business along that line of railway, that the Canadian Pacific Railway which has been operating it for the owning company headed by the member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) could not find any encouragement to make betterments upon the road, and it got into such a condition that it was almost dangerous to travel upon it. I say it again, and I say it advisedly, that had not that arrangement been made the railway would be at this moment out of commission. Hon. gentlemen opposite, in the attitude they have taken to-night, are quite consistent with their previous political history. It reminds me that some years ago when Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke at the board of trade banquet in Toronto after the Conservative Minister of Finance who had read long pages of statistics to prove that Canada was prosperous. Sir Wilfrid remarked that if he were at the head of the government and wished to prove that prosperity prevailed, he would ask the people to put their hands in their pockets to find whether prosperity existed. Our friends on the other side of the House still prefer to quote statistics and to hunt up departmental records, but for my part I prefer to go into the country and see the existence of prosperity
along that line of railway, where only three or four years ago there was nothing but desolation. To-day you can see thriving towns with hundreds of people doing a prosperous business. It is only four years ago this fall that my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Ross) and myself took a trip along that railway to that little ranching district of Dundurn. There was a building called Dundurn station, but no agent and no operator, and we had to wait on the railway line from ten o'clock in the morning till well after dark before we could get a train. There was no agent and no operator to give information, and we dare not leave the railway track for fear the train might come along at any moment. I was up there again a year ago last winter after this arrangement had been made with the Saskatchewan Land Company, and there was an agent at Dundurn station and I suppose a dozen large buildings, where a few months before there was nothing to in-dicatae business or prosperity. This Saskatchewan Yalley Land Company arrangement, taken by itself, has proved perhaps the most effective and successful of all the measures of the Minister of the Interior towards North-west progress.

The argument of the hon. member (Mr. Scott) is rather amusing, because it is not so long ago that we heard him declare in this House, that this railway line was so inefficient that it prevented settlers from going into the country. Tonight he says that but for this land deal that railway would not be a paying concern. He now contrasts the policy of the present government with the policy of the late government, and he says that because of the policy of this government there were thriving and prosperous towns and fertile country districts settled by farmers. If the land there was bad, it would not be settled with prosperous farmers ; you would not i find settlers take up their homesteads on land of such inferior quality as he described this land to be.

I have not said that the land is bad ; I do not think it is. It is perhaps not as good as in some other sections of the country. There may be certain sections of it not particularly good, but I do not wish to be understood as saying that the land is bad. I believe that a very large portion of the land in that district may be found to be very good indeed.
Why, five minutes ago the hon. gentleman said that the land was so bad, that the railway company went into the Exchequer Court to try to get out of taking it.

They said it was bad ; I did
not say so.

The hon. gentleman said that these shrewd railway men after send-

ing their agents to inspect the land, actually refused to take it because it was so bad.
I did not say so; they did.

And yet a few minutes afterwards the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) gets up and says that owing to the salu-tory policy of the government, there are rich and prosperous farmers settled on this land. It is quite plain that there is a nigger on the fence, and that any argument the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) may present to the House in regard to that section of the country must be taken at a discount. He has a peculiar kind of hydrophobia, which, whenever the member for Toronto or that railway company is mentioned, causes him to jump up in his seat as if he were worked by a spring, to denounce that hon. gentleman and the railway company with which he is connected. He places at his service any argument that accidentally comes into his mind on the impulse of the moment, regardless of whether it is logical or not, or whether it is in accord with the argument he presented a few moments before. He has given an example of that tonight. In my judgment the argument which he gives on one side and then on another makes his testimony of very little value to the country.

From what I have heard of the operations of this company in [DOT]this House and in another place, flhere does seem to be something very remarkable about it. The minister tells us that out of 3,500,000 acres of land, those who constructed the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, now operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, had the opportunity of selecting 800,000 acres. After the selection of that quantity, there would still be 2,100,000 acres. I understand that the Saskatchewan Land Company purchased from tne government 250,000 acres at the miserably low price of one dollar an acre, and that they did not get the poorest land, but had the privilege of selecting the 250,;-000 acres out of half a million acres. Is it likely that these shrewd American speculators, who went up there and pulled the wool over the minister's eyes and got such a bargain, were going to take the poorest land, when the fact is that they were getting selected land ? It has not yet been explained to me. why the government would allow an American company to go into a tract of land of 500.000 acres and pick out
250,000	acres of the best land they could get, and then hand it over to them for a dollar an acre, and receive payment in scrip, which, as the hon. gentleman for Marquette Says, possibly did not cost them more than fifty cents on the dollar. It looks to me like a huge job. In the first place, I do not think the Minister of the Interior should have the pow)er to sell the lands of that . western Mr. SPROULE.
country to any company at a dollar an acre. In my ignorance I thought it was the policy of the Liberal party to keep the laud for the settler. We heard that years ago ; but when these gentlemen get into power, it is the land for the speculator, and at Hie miserably low price of a dollar an acre, while the settler has to pay $5, $6 and1 $7 an acre for it. Well, this is not the first time that the Liberals have abandoned the policy they preached all over the country. It is only a sample case, but to my mind it is one of the dirtiest samples ever exposed in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I want to correct a remark I made a moment ago. When speaking of Fne sale of lands to the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company, I said that the price was $1.75 an acre. It was $1.53 an acre.

Now that the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) has indulged his monomaniac propensity to have his periodical fling at the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), that being evidently the object for which he rose to his feet, I would like to ask the minister if Mr. Pierce is still inspector of surveys ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Have any surveys been conducted in the Peace River country in the past year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There have been some block outline surveys, and one small tract has been subdivided.
Dominion lands, chargeable to income-commissioner's salary, $3,200.
There is an increase there.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There has been a general increase in the salaries of the civil servants, and this is not as large proportionately . as the increases of other officials.
There is a new official.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, J. W. Greenway, formerly inspector of school lands.
Dominion lands-superintendent of mines, $3,000.
What are the duties of. ths superintendent of mines

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The superintendent of mines during the last year has been engaged largely in the development of the system of examining ore deposits by the Swedish method. He published a work on that subject last year in order that mining institutes might post themselves on the matter. The hon. gentleman knows that there are vast deposits of iron in Canada. The work has been very highly commended by scientific mining bodies all over the world. Latterly

I appointed him to go to Europe at t'he head of a commission for the purpose of investigating the process of melting by electricity, and his report on that subject 'will be issued in the course of a week.
Is the Department of the Superintendent of Mines established by statute ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The office was created by statute many years ago.

I notice in last year's ' Hansard ' that the Prime Minister said, in reference to the superintendent of mining :
There is no doubt that with this amount of money voted by parliament the government has perfect authority to create such a work, but it will last only one year. Unless it is provided next year it will lapse, ipso facto ; it cannot be continued from year to year as it could if it were established by statute.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to a special vote for the superintendent of mines. The office was established years ago by statute. In the actual organization, we have not got the accommodation for the work he is carrying on, which is very largely laboratory work and requires scientific apparatus.
How many men has he under him ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He brings in specialists from time to time. We had to secure an electrical expert from Peterborough and a metallurgical expert from England to assist the investigations in Europe.
Is not the position of superintendent of mines a provisional position, or has the Dominion mines of its own which require a superintendent ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have the direct supervision of the mining territory upon Dominion lands, but the office he holds is for the purpose of carrying on investigations of a general character.

I would like to ask how it comes that Dr. Bell has not been gazetted as the head of the geological survey ? He has filled the position now four years and deserves every consideration, and I think some explanation should be given why he has not been permanently appointed. He is only receiving a salary of $2,400.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am responsible for making the appointment and am not prepared to recommend Dr. Bell. I have personally very kindly feelings towards him. He is the senior officer of the survey, and I appointed him the acting head in the hope that I would be able to make his position permanent but have not been able to do so. I prefer not to make any statement further than this, and my hon. friend will know that the question of the qualifications of
scientific men is a very difficult one for anybody who is not an expart himself.
If Dr. Bell is not fitted for the position, how comes it he has been kept in it for four years ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have had the reorganization of the department in contemplation for the past two or three years, and next year hope to be able to complete it, but so far have not been in a position to do so.
Who is the superintendent of mines ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. Haanel.
What was the result of his trip to Germany about the use of electricity in smelting ore ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The report will be ready for the printer in a couple of weeks, and I shall have much pleasure in sending a copy to each member of the House. I could not state satisfactorily in a few words the results of his report. If I entered into very full details, I might say something which might be misleading. The reason of the delay in getting out the report is because we only received the report of the metallurgical expert from England, who was appointed to examine into and make an analysis of the different processes of manufacture of steel, a short time ago.
Can the hon. minister not say in a general way whether the process is a success or a failure ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Speaking generally, it may be said that the report is encouraging and will demonstrate that given satisfactory qualities of ore and reasonably cheap power, electric smelting can be carried on successfully in some parts of Canada.

There is not much enlightenment in that. Given fairly good quality of ore and plenty of heat, you can smelt the ore. That follows as a matter of course. What experience has Dr. Haanel had to justify his being regarded as an expert in that line ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has the experience of a practical chemist and practical electrician.
Where did he gain his experience ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In a German university.

My information is that his only experience has been gained in study at the university. It is one thing to study and another to apply the theories you have learned at a university. It requires years of practical experience to make an expert.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, the government cannot have experts in every line. All the government can look for is a man who has

more or less general attainments, and when any special questions come up, he engages specialists from time to time. We have had an expert electrician from the Canadian General Electric Works at Peterborough, and a metallurgist from England recommended by competent authorities there. No government could keep in its employ men who were specialists in the different branches, with regard to which inquiry from time to time may have to be made. All we can do is engage specialists as they are required. At present we are contemplating making an inquiry into zinc in British Columbia, and we shall have to engage a man who is a zinc expert. What we want for a superintendent is not a man who is in the ordinary sense a specialist in any particular branch, but, a man of general scientific education, who will be able to direct particular inquiries.

I would not regard such a man as an expert at all. An expert is a man who has acquired special knowledge of a subject by the experience of a long time, and who puts that knowledge into practice. I am informed that Dr. Haanel is only a very commonplace man in his line, and was regarded in every line of life as rather a failure. But he is trotted out as an expert and is given a salary as an expert, being placed over the heads of other men in his line. I am informed that among other occupations he was in the ministerial line, but whether he was a success or not in that line I do not know. I do not think that this man will impress the intelligent people of the world.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When he was appointed he was professor of physics in Cornell University at Syracuse.

X would like to say a few words on behalf of Dr. Bell. I certainly am surprised to hear that he is not likely to receive the appointment of the Director of the Geological Survey. For forty-eight years Dr. Bell has been travelling throughout this country gaining information, and certainly he is a fountain of information with reference to the mines and topographical work of this country. He undoubtedly deserves the greatest credit from the people of this country. I have read his reports for years, and when we consider the efforts he has put forth on behalf of the people of this country in developing their mines, their woodlands and their agricultural lands, I am sure there is not a man in the House but will feel sore when he realizes that Dr. Bell is to accept a position secondary to any man in this country. He has crept up step by step until be is one of the most eminent geologists in the world, I may say. to-day. It seems that a geeat injustice must have been done him, when we realize that he has been dragged along, year after year filling the position of Director or the Geological Survey of this country ably and Mr. SIFTON.
well. If he had not filled it properly, why was the position not filled by some one who was capable of doing so ? Now, at his time of life, after the efforts and labours he has put forth on behalf of this country, I ,say it is a shame and a disgrace that a man holding the position that he does in the scientific world, possessing his ability, should have to accept a secondary position.
Mr. iSIFTON. Does my hon. friend know that when his friends were in office Dr. Bell had been in the Geological Survey for over thirty years, and yet his friends appointed a young man over his head as Director of the Survey, a young man who had been only comparatively a few years in the service ? My hon. friend must know that while we all respect age and experience, something else besides age and experience is required. My hon. friend must remember when he comes to pass judgment in matters of this kind, that I have had better opportunities of understanding the situation than he has had. My hon. friend has had no experience in the administration of the department, but he must realize that after administering the department for several years and being! brought into daily contact with the details of Its operation, I am in a fairly good position to express an opinion in regard to such a matter, and that I could not possibly be animated by any other motive than a desire to do what would be fair to Dr. Bell. Nothing would be more pleasant to me than to appoint Dr. Bell, but the most pleasant thing is not always the most satisfactory thing. If I felt I could appoint Dr. Bell 1 would do so. My hon. friend must give me ci*edlt .for believing that the conclusion at which I have arrived is based on the facts that have been brought to my attention.

Might it not be fair to Dr. Bell to suggest what there is lacking in the man that he is not capable of carrying on the work of the department ? I feel the position keenly, because I have known Dr. Bell, through his work, for many, many years, and realize that he has been a most valuable man to this country.
What position does Dr Bell occupy in the department, and what is his salary ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is acting Director. He has filled that position since Dr. Dawson died about three years ago.
How long has he been in the department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has been forty years in the Geological Survey.
What salary does he get now ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: $3,200, I think.
I think it is only $2,300 now, and that he has not even had the statutory increases the last two years.
Has lie reached the maximum of his class, and what class is he in ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Officers of the Geological Survey are called technical officers, and their salaries are especially voted every year. At the time Dr. Bell was appointed acting Director he was getting $2,400 ; I am not sure whether he is now getting $3,200 or not, hut I think so. Of course, we are not now passing Geological Survey items, and I have not the papers under my hand. When we come to the items of the Geological Survey, I will he able to tell my hon. friend.
What salary was Dr. Dawson getting at the time of his death ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Has Dr. Bell been getting that salary while performing the duties since Dr. Dawson's death ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: During the first two years he did not receive the full salary, and I remember that the reason why he did not was that the question had come up upon various occasions as to whether officers ot the government filling higher positions temporarily should receive the salaries of the officers for whom they were acting. I sent it before the council for the purpose of being discussed, and that was the decision that was arrived at.
What class is Dr. Bell in at the present time? The minister's statement is very indefinite regarding the salary. He says he thinks he gets $3,200.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is not in any class. The officers of the Geological Survey are not classified as are the officers of the civil service. They are rated as technical officials and their salaries are specially voted.
In the Auditor General's Report he appears to get $2,400.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said the salary of the director was $3,200. The question whether Dr. Bell was to get the salary of a director was up on one occasion and it was decided that he should not. I do not remember whether be has been getting it this last year.

It is quite clear that he has not. By the Auditor General's Report he has been getting $2,400. It would be interesting to know why he has not been getting more. Ever since his predecessor died I suppose he has been getting the same salary. The statutory increase, I presume, would not apply to him, if he does not come under the Civil Service Act, though as a technical officer, he would be eligible for the statutory increase there as well. It would be interesting to know when his salary was increased, and to what extent, during the past few years. I have heard it said that he gets a much smaller salary in proportion than others who are doing equally valuable work, and that in addition be is not a permanent appointment, that some one else might be put over his head at any time. I assume from what the minister says that he is not likely to appoint him. It appears that he has been in the service for 48 years.

I must say that a salary of $2,400 for an officer who has been 48 years in tbe service of the government, affords little encouragement to men of talent and scientific ability to engage in the service of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not responsible for the scale of salaries in the Geological Survey.
I do not think the hon. gentleman ought to ask me, in the case of a gentleman who has occupied the position of a scientific man in that department for the last 40 years, why I do not think lie is a desirable man to put at the head of that department. I think he is a very respectable gentleman, and performs valuable public service, but if I remain in office and endeavour' to put the Geological Survey on a much more useful basis, I do not think he is a good man for the position and would not recommend him.

I understood the minister to infer in his answer to the hon. member for Lambton that he was not a suitable man for tbe position.
