Then we have the fact that the minister brings in a new man who has had no experience at all, and gives him $3,000 a year, Dr. Haanel, without any experience, and no other qualification as disclosed to us except that he was a schoolmate of the minister when they were at college. Now it does seem to me that this is the old story tbat kissing goes by favour. The minister puts a friend of his in a high position, without any knowledge upon which to base his judgment; he puts him into this position, and gives him a salary over and above a man who has rendered faithful service for 48 years, and whose education so far as we krnvw bas been all that a man should require to make him an expert. In addition to that, he has had training and experience for that length of time, yet a new man is brought in without any experience at all, and put over him and given a larger salary.
Mi-. SIFTON. No new man is put over him at all.
Because Dr. Haanel is given a higher salary, therefore .lie must have a higher position.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Dr. Haanel has nothing to do with the Geological Survey at all. His duties are connected solely with metallurgy.
Salaries of inspectors, Dominion lands and Crown timber agents, sub-agents and clerks in the outside service, $121,700.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I v^is speaking of a general increase in salaries under the amended Civil Service Act. We have made some increases for officials who were not affected by that amended Act, not as a result of or by the action of that amendment, but because of the fact that the salaries ought to he somewhat Increased. A certain scale of increase was provided for those who were affected by the Act. Rut I had no reference to officials Of the class my hon. friend refers to in the outside service. I have an impression that the gentleman my hon. friend refers to is a very old man.
He is old, but he is very active.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My impression was that he is an old man, and that the clerk did most of the work. If my hon. friend thinks, he is deserving I am quite prepared to consider it. He has 'had the same salary for a long time.

The clerk's salary was increased from $780 to $1,000, but the head of the office, Mr. Flesher, remains at the same salary. Mr. Flesher is a very active man. He is up in years but he never misses a day from his office. He does the greater portion of the work notwithstanding that the clerk is much younger. I am not complaining that the salary of the clerk was increased but I consider that if his salary was increased Mr. Flesher is entitled to have his increased as well. .

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will look into it.

In view of the fact that before another session we will be in the throes of an election campaign, I think the hon. minister will be aggrieved to hear that some of his officials, inspectors, Ac., have been taking a very active part politically.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When ?

They are doing it at the present time.
Mr. SIFTON Will the hon. gentleman specify ?

Yes. A year ago a question in regard to civil servants taking Mr. SIFTON.
part in elections in Manitoba came up for discussion in this House when the hon. minister wras not present. I brought to the attention of the House the specific case of Mr. Thos. Young, homestead inspector at Dauphin. His case was one which the right hon. Prime Minister stated came within the rule which he had laid down. The right hon. gentleman stated that if he accepted the nomination of the Liberal party for the Manitoba legislature he would cease to be an employee of the Dominion government. Mr. Thos. Young at that time did accept the nomination on behalf of the Liberal party. I pointed out to the House that I felt confident what was going to be the result, that Mr. Young was being allowed to retire temporarily during the campaign and that when the campaign was over and the elections consigned him to private life again he would be appointed to his position. I tried to get some specific declaration from the acting minister as to whether that procedure would be followed or not. The reason I was so sceptical in regard to the action that the government would take was that the same thing happened in my own constituency where my opponent in the last election who had been homestead inspector was allowed to resign to take part in the contest and who, after being defeated, was reappointed to his position. I instanced that as an illustration that most likely that procedure would be followed in the case of Mr. Young. On the 6lh of April in this House I asked the hon. minister the following question ?
1. Did (Mr. Thos. Young, homestead inspector, Manitoba, resign his position during the year 1903 ?
The reply was :
Yes.
The second question was :
If so, what was the date of his resignation ?
The answer was :
12th July, 1903.
I may say that that was the very day upon which I was personally present at a political meeting where Mr. Thos. Young had spoken from the same platform as I myself had been speaking from. Yet, he resigned on the 12th July. The third question was :
Was Mr. Young a candidate at the provincial elections in Manitoba last July ?
This is the very innocent answer which the hon. gentleman gave :
The department has no information on this point. He was reported in the press as being a candidate.
I think the hon. minister is not nearly so innocent as he would imply by that answer, because I read Mr. Thos. Young's acceptance of the nomination last year. That

ought to be official enough. So official was it that the right hon. Prime Minister recognized this ease as coming within the rule laid down and as constituting an infringement of a civil servant's proper duties and declared that he should be asked to retire. The fourth question was :
Is Mr. Young now in the employ of the government ? If so, in what capacity ; what is the date of his appointment, and the amount of his salary ?
The answer was :
Yes, Mr. Young is now employed as forest ranger for northwestern Manitoba. He was appointed on the 9th November, 1903, at $125 per month.
So that, the very thing that I predicted would happen, did come to pass. Not only was Mr. Thos. Young reappointed, but he was reappointed at an increased salary to soothe his wounded feelings for having been defeated in the previous contest. He had been prior to the time he resigned in receipt of a salary of $100 a month and he was reappointed at the rate of $125 a month no doubt to recompense him for the loss of time consequent upon the campaign. [DOT]
He had had more experience.

Yes, he was a sadder and a wiser man. This same Mr. Thos. Young to-day is a most active politician and no person in that part of the country be he Liberal or Conservative, will say anything to the contrary. But, Mr. Thos. Young is not the only one. There is a gentleman named Yeo, a land agent in the Emerson district whose particular duty seems to be to look after the Galicians. Mr. Yeo was the party who was put in charge of bringing the Galicians out last y*ear to register. They were not then qualified to register. He brought them out a month ago to register.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is a sub-land agent. The men whd are appointed as sub-land agents are given small salaries, are not supposed to devote their whole time to the service and are not therefore in the ordinary sense government agents.
It appears that the hon. gentleman discriminates according to the amount of salary his officers get.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He only gets $25 a month.
There is another official, Mr Harvey. I think he is supposed to be an interpreter. Would the hon. gentleman inform us what Mr. Harvey's duties are supposed to be ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My deputy informs me he is an interpreter at Winnipeg.
What is his particular duty ?
He is in the immigration service.
What does he do ? Does he accompany parties of foreigners around and interpret V

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The interpreters are there for the purpose of being in communication with foreign settlers when they come in. He interprets for the foreign settlers when they come in and he is also sent out with settlers to assist them in making locations.

He accompanies foreigners to their new locations. I wish to direct the hon. minister's attention to the fact that Mr. Harvey has been during the past two or three months devoting his time and attention to my humble self.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What has he been doing?

He is acting as interpreter for the Liberal candidate in his canvass. I do not know whether it comes within the scope of his duties or not but it is a notorious fact that Mr. Harvey has accompanied from house to house Mr. S. L. Head, the Liberal candidate for Marquette interpreting for the Galicians. I do not thiiik it is the duty of this gentleman to accompany any candidate, Grit or Tory because he is paid by Conservative money as well as Liberal money and I do not think the hon. Minister of the Interior will defend any such action on his part. I have not the slightest doubt that when I draw the attention of the hon. minister to his conduct he will have this gentleman summarily dismissed, because we know that other officials have been dismissed upon the representations made by hon. members of this House. I can assure him that what I am telling him is a fact because' if it were not a fact I would be the last one to say so. The fact is that he has been accompanying the Liberal candidate from House to House, in the Galician settlement acting as interpreter and one old Galician in his quaint way, describing his actions and manners afterwards, said that he put him in mind of a man spreading butter very thickly on bread. I wish to draw the hon. minister's attention to this fact and I am sure that he will have this gentleman's conduct inquired into. I do not ask that this gentleman- shall be decapitated without being given an opportunity to present his defence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will not undertake to dispute what my hon. friend says. It certainly is not the business of an official of the immigration department to travel around with any candidate or to act as an interpreter for him. I cannot say that I have in my mind the names of all the officials of the service and I was not aware that a man by the name of Harvey was there. My deputy informs me that lie is an interpreter. This is the first I have heard of the matter to which my hon. friend refers and I will

give instructions to have the matter investigated. The instructions will [DOT] be not only to him but to other officials in the service.

It would hardly be expected that the minister would remember the names because their names are legion.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I may point out that all the Conservative members in Manitoba would appear to have had their own experience with regard to this state of things. There was a Liberal convention in my riding last fall when the election was expected, and several aspiring Liberal candidates appeared on the scene. It is said, that at the convention, a government official who was one of the scrutineers worked the thing in such a way, that he turned the wheel in favour of the candidate who did not have a majority of the votes.

He switched.
Mr. LaRIYIERE. I may say that two of the aspiring Liberal candidates were government officials. One was an old official who has been in and out of the local legislature, and who when out of the legislature is a regular official of the government, and when in the legislature is paid by the day. This official had his name on the list of candidates presented at the convention, but the wheel of fortune was turned over to an official of the Public Works Department, and who is now supposed to be the Liberal candidate. Candidate No. 1 was dissatisfied and complained that he had been robbed of the convention, and so the fortunate candidate had to come down to Ottawa to complain that his brother official was interfering with his chances of election. The unlucky candidate was called down to Ottawa and the Deputy Minister of the Interior made him an offer to go to France on an immigration mission, so that he might be away during election time and not hamper his Liberal friend. This official did go to France but no election took place, and the other candidate has had to resume his work in the Public Works Department. The aspiring candidate who had been robbed of the convention had to come back from France and he had to cable and cable for money to enable him to do so. The government it would appear did not want to see him again, but at all events after very considerable delay he managed to get enough money to take him to his home. He has now resumed his duties in the Dominion Lands Department in Winnipeg as an inspector of something, and we are awaiting the election. I might say that at that convention held by the Liberals of St. Boniface-as a matter of fact there were three conventions but I refer to the last-there were no less than twenty officials of the Dominion government attending the convention to select a candidate to oppose me and to try to defeat me at the coining election.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: They have a big contract on hand.

The Minister of the Interior and some of his supporters seem to look upon this as rather amusing, judging from their smiles, but if they had been here from 1893 to 1896 and had listened to the castigation handed out to the Conservative government if an official interfered remotely in an election (not to speak of the flagrant interference of the present officials of the Interior Department), these hon. members would have a different smile upon their faces from what we see to-night. We all remember that last session we brought to the attention of the government the fact that a number of the officials of the Interior Department were taking a very active part in the local elections, that they were in fact Liberal candidates, and we predicted that after their defeat they would resume their positions. That prediction has been verified. As the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) has forcibly drawn to the attention of the minister, his officials are again taking a prominent part in the political struggle. It is most unfair to permit these officials who receive their pay from the country as a whole, to participate in political contests. I am surprised that the Minister of Interior, who when he is at home gets the credit of going into the fight fairly and fearlessly, should allow such underhand conduct as this. It has been said that he could not get Liberal candidates unless he looked for them in the ranks of his officials, but I venture to think that if he paused and thought about it a little, he would put an end to this indecent state of things. It is now said that three or four of the Liberal candidates in the field are identified with the Saskatchewan Land Company, beginning with Mr. MacKenzie up in Alberta and going along to Mr. Dawson and Mr. Turriff and right down pretty nearly along the whole line, that is the rumour: the minister may not hear it but it is talked about and even written about in the newspapers. If the, minister did his duty, or had any desire to see fair play he would put a stop to these officials interfering in politics.

Before this item passes, there is a matter I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of the Interior in reference to a dispute between certain sections of the Galician people in township 18 range 3. I will state the circumstances so that the minister may take them into consideration. It appears that three years ago Father Philas. head of the Order of Basilians in Manitoba 'and the Northwest Territories, made application for a homestead entry of legal subdivision 16 of section 27, township 18, range 3 east. The application was made for the Greek Catholic church and $10 entry fee wras paid. A receipt was given for the entry fee and the entry was made in the books of the

Dominion Lands Office. The Greek Catholics then proceeded to build a church on the property which cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $500, and at a meeting of the Greek Catholics of that district five trustees were elected to look after the property on behalf of the congregation. Everything went along all right until about "a year ago, when some priests of the Independent Greek Church-another branch of the Greek Church-went into the district and succeeded in getting two of the trustees to leave the Greek Catholic Church and come over to the Independent Church. They then formed a congregation known as the Greek Independent Church and took forcible possession of the church which the Greek Catholics had erected. When the Greek Catho-olics found that two of their trustees had deserted and gone over to the enemy, they held another meeting and elected two other trustees to till their places. The five trustees of the Greek Catholic Church then caused the church to be locked, but the Independent Greek Church Congregation or some one acting on their behalf, forced the lock and took possession. Matters have been going on in this way ever since, and Father Phi-las went to the Dominion Lands Office and made a complaint against the action of the Independent Greek Church, and he was promised that matters would be investigated. He called at the land office in Winnipeg a few days ago, and was informed that a Mr. Foley, one of the homestead inspectors had been sent out to the district to investigate, and had sent in a report on the basis of which the department had decided to issue a patent to the Independent Greek Church trustees.
The Greek Catholic trustees were not notified that Mr. Foley was going out into that district, and they were therefore not consulted by him while he was out there. If the state of affairs is as represented to me -and I have every reason to believe it is, for I have been informed by Father Filas himself-it seems to have been a very highhanded proceeding on the part of the government to act on the report of one of their officials who only consulted one side of the arrangement, and did not consult those who contributed their money to build the church. I would ask the minister to investigate the case at the earliest possible moment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know the circumstances of the case, but it is of sufficient importance to warrant us in finding out what both parties have to say, and I will have It investigated.
Salaries of extra clerks at head office and advertising, including $5,000 for extra service in connection with Dominion lands, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $38,500.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Does this advertising include the advertising of land regulations and mining regulations ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not altogether.
What is the increase of $11,000 for ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The details of the increase are as follows :	In connection with the
Dominion Lands Branch there have been eighteen additional appointments of the writer class, whose salaries altogether amount to $10,175 ; there are statutory increases for two clerks, amounting to $105 ; there have been Increases in the salaries of clerks and messengers under the provisions of the amendment of the Civil Service Act of last year, amounting altogether to $3,860 ; and there is an increase in the amount for advertising and printing of $3,100 making a total of $17,000 odd. There have been decreases by the appointment of four clerks of the temporary staff, paid out of this vote, to the permanent staff as junior second-class clerks. Two temporary clerks have been made permanent. Four clerks have been transferred from this to another branch. One has resigned from the service, which makes a saving of about $6,000 or a net increase of $11,000 in the vote.
Dominion Lands-protection of timber lands in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, and tree culture in the Northwest Territories, $40,000.

What are the regulations regarding portable saw-mills ? I understand that, as they are enforced ii* the Dominion reserves at Dauphin, farmers are not permitted to have portable saw-mills set up within the reserve, and must haul their logs some miles to have them sawn. 'They object to that seriously.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The farmers are not supposed to have portable saw-mills. My hon. friend knows the practice better than I do. The practice followed Is this. People set up portable saw-mills for the farmers who get permission to take out logs for their houses.
X have a fairly good idea that what is being done is perhaps not altogether within the spirit of the regulations, but the net result is that the new settlers are getting their timber for building purposes the cheapest way they can, and I do not think that public policy requires the practice to be interfered with. As a matter of fact, the regulations do not contemplate the farmers setting up portable saw-mills. They are supposed to take out a certain number of logs for the purpose of building their bouses and not more.
Are they not permitted to saw logs to build a frame house ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A man would not likely set up a portable saw-mill just to cut up logs for one house. A number of people club together and a portable saw-mill is set up.

Suppose a number of people club together and have one port-



able saw-mill set up by one of the farmers who saws for all the rest, what is the objection ? The hon. gentleman has his officials to see that they do not cut up the logs for sale. Is it not a fact that some of those timber reserve lands were surveyed a few years ago ? Have none of the timber reserves been sub-divided ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not so far as I know.
What has 'been done with regard to tree culture ? Who is doing that work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is being done on the plan I explained to the House during the last two or three years, under the supervision *of Mr. Stewart. The free distribution of frees in Manitoba is not being carried on to as great an extent as heretofore. Private individuals are now going into the business of furnishing seedlings, and in a short time the free distribution may cease. In the Territories, however, it is necessary to continue it on a large scale. If my hon. friend would take the trouble to look up the report of the chief of the forestry branch, he will see what is being done. For the year 1904, in the province of Manitoba, 1,200,000 young trees were furnished, and in the Territories 500,000, so that for this year 1,700,000 have been furnished.
I thought these were furnished by the experimental farms.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We raised some of them on the experimental farms. At Indian Head we have purchased a small plot of ground, upon which we intend to raise seedlings.
Where did you get the million of trees planted out ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We raised them from the seed.
I understood that the work was being done by the experimental farm. We have money voted for the purposes of that farm, why put an item in here to duplicate the same work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We raise the seedlings on the experimental farms.

Where have you plantations outside the experimental farm ?
Mi-. SIFTON. We have 160 acres at Indian Head, which are not upon the experimental farm, but a particular place set apart for the purpose of raising seedlings.
Is that the only place ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, outside the farm.
How much of this money is intended for that work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is the total vote for the whole service. The expenses in connection with the shrubbery are set down in the superintendent's estimate as $3,405, paid out of this vote.
Mr. W- J. ROCHE.

I have never understood that thei-e was any tree culture outside of the experimental farm, and that the seed sown there was given out to the farmers generally. I cannot understand why yon have an item here for that purpose. I cannot understand why we would require an item here for that purpose when we vote money enough to carry on the work of the farm.
, Mr. SIFTON. This is a special branch. The work might have been carried on by the Department of Agriculture as a part of its work, hut it was determined to do it in my department. The cost is the same ; if the Minister of Agriculture were doing it he would have to ask so much more money than he does. There is a small plot of land at the experimental farm of which our men are making use.
This is another instance c|f that duplicating which is done and it would seem that sometimes the object of it is to provide work for some one.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The farm is not doing this work at all.
Mr. SPROULE-"Then- wliat are they spending the money for ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is not an appropriation for the experimental farm ; it is an appropriation for the forestry branch ; the officers of the forestry branch make use of a small amount of land on the farms to do this work.

You employ a Mr. Stewart as timber inspector or something of that kind and now Mr. Stewart is starting to scratch up little patches on the-experimental farm and sow seeds. At the same time we have a staff at the experimental farm who are doing that work. Tire same thing prevails in other lines, as for example, in the case of the chicken fattening stations, some of which are apparently started simply to give a little patronage to friends, but there are very little returns from them. If we want to go Into the cultivation of trees in connection with the farm or not, do it at one place in the Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is exactly what we are doing. We started this work at the farm because that was the most convenient way pf doing it and we wanted to get on with the work, and as the result of our experience we have established a small place in the neighbourhood of Indian Head where we Intend to carry on the work exclusively.
This item is so worked that we are not able to judge of tlie different purposes for which it is intended. Where is Mr. Stewart located permanently?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: If Mr. Stewart has his headquarters here is he more likely to be successful in carrying on tree planting at Indian Head, than a man in charge of the farm there who has been doing the work lor years ? How much of this vote is used for fire protection and how much for tree planting ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:

That does not give any information ; this item refers only to Manitoba and the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It should include British Columbia.
225J

In addition to that the minister has it all mixed up, part of it for fire protection, part of it for tree culture, part of it for farms and part of it for other lines, so that we are as much in the dark as ever. We should not have them all put together so that we cannot ascertain what is being spent on these different items in order that we may judge whether the criticism is what it should be or not.. If we had the work that took place on the farm and the number of officers employed, we would be in a better position to judge intelligently of this expenditure, but it is all jumbled up, two or t'kree things together and we cannot separate it so that it can be properly analysed. I think that ought to be done for the benefit of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will note that I gave the figures of the $12,000 for the payment of four fire rangers in respect of Dominion lands.
Is all the rest of that for tree culture ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Substantially, yes. It includes the salaries of officers who take charge of this fire protection.
Miscellaneous-maintenance, construction of roads, bridges and other necessary -works in connection with the Hot Springs Reservation near Banff Station, Northwest Territories, $27,020.
Is there anything in the report of the Interior Department showing what is being done from year to year at Banff ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a report every year to the head of the department which show's what has been done, it is printed in the departmental report. This vote is required for payment of salaries, caretakers, repairs for roads, bridge over the river, purchase of animals, new roads, clearing land. The report of the superintendent is found on page 25 of last year's departmental report.
Under whose supervision is this work done, or is it done by day labour ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Most of it is done by day work under the supervision of the superintendent. The museum that wras put up a year ago wras of course built by contract, but nearly all the work of building bridges and repairing roads is done by day labour. That is found to be the cheaper and more satisfactory way of doing it. If my hon. friend has had the pleasure of visiting the park he has found that some of the best road-making done in Canada has been done in that part. The superintendent has done marvellously good work for the amount of money at his disposal.
What kind of animals do you intend to buy ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have bought goats, bulls, four or five elks. The superintendent has been endeavouring to get specimens of the mountain sheep. He has been trying to get a couple of buffalos from the far north within the past two or three years, but he has not succeeded yet, and I have practically given up further attempts. The report shows that at the present time we have forty buffalos, eight elk. four deer, fourteen angora goats, besides moose and some other animals. Three buffalos were presented by Mr. T. G. Blackstock, of Toronto, and fifteen or sixteen were presented to the government by Lord Strathcona. The others have been bought from time to time within the last five or six years.
We are voting an item to be used the present year, and I think we voted the same item last year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We take this estimate so that the superintendent may have the money in case he desires to use it.
How much of that vote last year was spent for the purpose of buying animals ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Auditor General's Report of last year only shows an expenditure of $79.50.
Was it for the purpose of supplying this park that the hon. gentleman got his hon. friend the Minister of Finance to put goats on the free list ?
They are going to Ontario.
They need not send goats to the Northwest. I ask the hon. minister where he got the goats ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are a rather rare breed of goats.
Miscellaneous-construction of roads, bridle paths and other necessary works in connection with the Yoho park reserve and immediate vicinity, $10,000.
Where is this park ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yoho Park is a continuation of the Banff park. The Banff park runs up to the British Columbia line and in the railway belt, beyond the British Columbia line, we have set apart a park contiguous to the Rocky Mountain park. Yoho park contains magnificent natural scenery and some glaciers which are declared to be equal to the Alpine glaciers. The Canadian Pacific Railway have spent a considerable amount of money in sending in experts for the purpose of definitely locating the glaciers and we are building bridle paths so as to make them accessible to tourists. They are a very great attraction to tourists going through to the coast The Canadian Pacific Railway have taken a great interest in developing the tourist business. We have done what we Mr. SPROULE.
could to make the park attractive and accessible. This particular vote is for the construction of a road from Field to Taka-kaw Falls including two bridges across the Yoho river, $9,000 repairs to tote road, Field to Hector, $300 ; repairs from Field to Ottertail, $500 ; trail from Emerhld lake to Burgess Pass. $400; trail from Emerald lake to Glacier. $150 ;[DOT] extension natural bridge to Canyon, $100 ; a total of $10,450. We are asking for $10,000.
How is that work being done ? Have you another staff of men there and if so, how many of them ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, there is no staff there. This is part of the other park. The difference is only in the name.
Do you not think it would be better to put the whole of it under one vote ? What object is there in dividing it up ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is across the British Columbia line : that is all. What is known as the Rocky Mountain park is taken out of the Northwest Territories and is under the legislative jurisdiction of this Federal parliament. In British Columbia we own the park only as a private individual might own land. We own that much land there so there is a difference in the legal position in which we are placed. There would be no objection to calling it Banff park but at the time the park was established Yoho was suggested and it was given that name.
When you own the property, as a private individual would own it, why do you require to divide it up and have one item of $10,000 for this park and another item of $27,000 for the other park ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is exactly the same as if we had it under one name.
Perhaps if you had one item it would be a larger vote than if you divided it up into two smaller items.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The roads would cost the same.

The roads would cost the same but when we take up the Auditor General's Report to ascertain what expenditure has taken place to embellish this park you have to look under two different names to find it. Persons not familiar with the circumstances, not having heard the explanation of the minister, would not be likely to find out what the expenditure had been. They would look for Banff park and they would see the expenditure that had taken place there but they would not know that there is another park which is an addition to this same park.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon friend will bring in a Bill to put ft under one name I will' vote for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of this vote of $63,000, $43,000 is required, for the operations on the 49th parallel west of the Rocky Mountains. Including salaries of surveyors and assistants engaged thereon. This work is being carried on under the agreement between the British and United States governments. It will consist of running the line and cutting out a vista throughout, cutting the necessary trails, making a triangulation to measure the distances, making a topographic survey of the adjacent country, taking necessary astronomical and other observations, and the purchase and placing of monuments to replace the existing mounds of loose stones. The estimated running expenses of the parties are $24,000, the salaries of surveyors and their professional assistants $11,000, and the cost of monuments, $8,000. In connection with the astronomical work the salaries amount to $12,580, and in connection with field astronomical work the estimate is $3,500. This last amount is to cover the expenses of observers engaged in the determination of latitudes and longitudes in the eastern provinces. Then, there are travelling expenses amounting to $900, and books, stationery, *&e., $3,020, making a total of $63,000.
That is for the boundary between our country and Alaska ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, there is nothing here for that We will have a supplementary vote for that.
Where is this work being done ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is for the actual surveying of the boundary, on the 49th parellel of British Columbia.
Between British Columbia and the United States ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is very expensive because of the fact that it is in a mountainous country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the position of the work at the present time ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will be able to answer that to-morrow.
How much was spent of last year's vote ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I am safe in saying it was all spent.
That is no information at all. I asked also how much of this work was done, and when it would be completed, and the minister could not answer that question either.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will have a statement prepared for my hon. friend to-morrow.
Miscellaneous-cost of litigation, $11,000.

At page L-57 of the Auditor General's Report I see an amount of $1,368.98 paid, to Howell, Mathers & Howell, which I believe is in connection with the litigation which took place on behalf of the municipalities of Argyle and Springdale regarding the school taxes. Would the minister explain what position that matter is now in ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is in the Department of Justice, and I would prefer to let the Minister of Justice do that. I think he read a statement in the House last session showing what the legal result was. I will call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the matter, and ask him to make a statement.
Are these lands paying the school taxes ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no doubt the school taxes are being levied against them in pursuance of that decision. If they are not paid I suppose the local government would sell them for taxes.
I do not think the government should allow lands set apart for schools to be sold for taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) does not perhaps understand. A suit was instituted for the purpose of determining whether the Canadian Pacific Railway was liable to taxation by the local municipal authorities. One suit was taken with respect to Manitoba and another with respect to the Northwest Territories, because the conditions were supposed to be different. I do not want to be held responsible for the exact legal correctness of what I say, but I understand it was held that in the Territories the land was liable for school taxes, and in reply to my hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) I said that under the local ordinances I presumed the school taxes were being levied, and if the taxes were not paid the lands could be sold.
Miscellaneous-maintenance of assay office, Vancouver, $13,000.

Are you doing less work there, to account for this decrease ?

7080'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The office was very much over-worked last year ; the work is not so great this year, and the expenses are less.
What staff have you, and their salaries ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The manager, $2,500 ; the assayer, $1,500 ; assistant assayer, $1,300 ; melter, $1,400 ; janitor, $950 ; and various other expenditures for supplies, &c.
Miscellaneous-engraving, lithographing and printing maps of Dominion and Northwest Territories, $15,000.
Did you issue any new maps last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A new map of the Northwest Territories was issued four or five months ago, and I will send my hon. friend half a dozen copies if he wishes.
I would like to see them. Are you sending out any more new maps this year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I make it a practice to send all these publications to the members, and I did not think about that one, or I would have issued instructions to send it out.
Does the hon. minister intend to get out any new maps this season, and if so, of what districts ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are carrying on the work of issuing new' sheets of different portions of the Dominion constantly, with new information. The particular vote for w'hieh I am asking is for four different sheets- one for the southwestern portion of Ontario, one for Quebec, one for New Brunswick, and one for southern British Columbia. This is in addition to reprinting some of the maps which we have with additional information up to date.
What are these maps intended to show-the geological deposits ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are not geological maps. They are maps of Canada. I have no doubt my hon. friend got a copy of the map of Canada which we issued a short time ago.

It was a mere outline map. Maps which would be valuable would be maps showing the railways, the land sold and the land unsold, the land settled and the land unsettled. So far as I know, there is no map of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The new map issued a year or so ago contained all the information which it was possible to put on a map. There was so much information on it that it had to be engraved on copper. A map showing where the land offices are and information of a similar kind would have to be published as a special map. It could not be put on a large map of the Dominion of Canada.
But yon are not getting out a large map of the Dominion of Canada. You are only getting out sectional maps.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will understand that the officers are perfecting the-geography of Canada, and are getting out a portion at a time.

The information does not go far enough. I asked whether it was a railway map, a land map or a geological map, or whether it contained all this information ? We sometimes have inquiries for maps of this kind. Where, for instance, can I get a railway map of the Northwest or British Columbia ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend can get a railway map by looking at the map of the Dominion of Canada which was issued last year.
Some resolutions reported.

speechtext: Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What work will be taken up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of the Interior will continue his estimates, to be followed by the Minister of Agriculture.
What line will the Minister of the Interior take up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Immigration.
The hon. gentleman cannot take up immigration until the report is down and we have some little time to consider it. We have not got it yet.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is nothing in the report except the evidence taken before the committee, and the hon. gentleman has had that. There is no use of holding up the estimates until the. evidence is sent down by the committee.
We are in this awkward dilemma, that the report is not before us, and we cannot discuss it until it is.
Can the Minister of Finance tell us whether the Minister of Justice intends to go on with his Railway Bill to-morrow ?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: As the Minister of Agriculture is not here, I give notice to the Minister of Finance that on the motion togo into Supply, I shall have something to say with reference to the report of the Department of Agriculture.
